[Graph engineering for AI factories](~/Documents/Engineering%20Enablement%20AI/research/graph-engineering-ai-factories-2026-07-29.md:1)

## Bottom line

The Slack thread’s progression is sound:

`AI factories → loop engineering → graph engineering`

But graph engineering is not the factory.

- Loop engineering governs one adaptive agent loop.
- Graph engineering composes loops, tools, deterministic checks, routing, parallel work, retries, and human gates.
- AI-factory engineering operates those graphs safely across durability, identity, evaluation, cost, versioning, governance, and release.

The core thesis is:

> The graph is the process topology. It is not the factory.

## Current state

“Graph engineering” is a very new label for an established architectural pattern. LangChain publicly framed the term on July 22, while acknowledging that graph-based agent orchestration has existed for years. Google ADK 2.0 has moved graph-first, AutoGen’s GraphFlow remains experimental, and OpenAI explicitly warns that declarative graphs become cumbersome as workflows grow dynamic and complex. [LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/3-years-of-graph-engineering-with-langgraph), [Google ADK](https://developers.googleblog.com/announcing-adk-go-20/), [OpenAI](https://openai.com/business/guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-ai-agents/)

There is currently:

- no shared definition of graph engineering;
- no portable cross-framework graph format;
- no standard checkpoint, reducer, replay, migration, or evaluation contract;
- substantial ambiguity with knowledge graphs, context graphs, lineage graphs, and model computation graphs.

The Slack sequence most plausibly means control-flow/stateful execution graphs, not knowledge graphs. The latter should remain a secondary topic because the AI Engineer ecosystem already treats “Graphs,” “Software Factories,” and “AI Factories” as separate territories.

## Architectural and scale limitations

The major problems are:

- **Topology is not semantics.** A deterministic edge can still lead to a nondeterministic model, stale context, an unsafe tool call, or an incorrect patch.
- **Execution graphs and information-flow graphs differ.** AutoGen, for example, separates its execution graph from its message graph. Controlling who runs next does not automatically control who sees which context.
- **Durability changes application semantics.** Resume and replay can re-execute model calls and external actions. Side effects require durable intent, idempotency keys, receipts, deduplication, and sometimes compensation.
- **Parallelism creates merge problems.** Fan-out introduces checkpoint conflicts, state reducers, conflicting patches, partial success, cancellation, and rate-limit pressure. Coding work is also less naturally parallel than research.
- **Static diagrams stop matching runtime reality.** Dynamic workers, model-selected routes, cycles, nested graphs, and late-bound tools make visual comprehensibility and exhaustive path testing difficult.
- **Observability is not evaluation.** A trace shows what ran; it does not prove that the route was justified, the patch was correct, or the workflow was economical.
- **Security extends through every node.** An allowed edge is not authorization. Persistent state and cross-tool execution add prompt injection, confused-deputy, credential, provenance, and secret-retention risks.
- **Human approval can become stale.** A paused graph may resume after the repository, policy, model, or target action has changed.
- **Costs are topology-dependent and stochastic.** Anthropic reports roughly 15× chat token usage in its multi-agent research workload and specifically notes that coding offers fewer truly parallelizable tasks. [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- **Live-run versioning is hard.** Graph topology, state schemas, prompts, models, tools, policies, and evaluators can all change while checkpoints remain active.
- **MCP and A2A do not solve graph portability.** They standardize capability access and agent communication, not internal orchestration or recovery semantics.

## Strongest summit direction

The lead proposal should be:

> **The Graph Is Not the Factory: Seven Systems Missing from Production Coding Agents**

This is stronger than “What Is Graph Engineering?” because it is a falsifiable production argument, not a category overview.

The two best additional proposals are:

1. **Replay Is a Side-Effect Bug: Idempotency for Long-Running Coding-Agent Graphs**
2. **When the Work Graph Changes Mid-Run: Versioning Stateful Coding Agents**

The submission should be backed by one representative coding workflow and injected failures: crash after an external write, concurrent patch conflict, stale approval, permission denial, token-budget exhaustion, and mid-run topology migration.

That evidence is the missing development work. The conceptual pieces already connect your existing separation-of-agentic-concerns, tracing, governed-autonomy, and executable-quality-gates material.

The CFP is open, accepts up to three proposals, reports a historical 5–15% acceptance rate, and primarily uses 15–20 minute stage talks. September 15 is the early-review target; October 11 is the final deadline. [Official event page](https://www.ai.engineer/code/2026), [official CFP](https://sessionize.com/aiecode26/)

No Slack message, content package, CFP submission, approval, or publication state was created.

> For the lead proposal, if I'm presenting problems then I need to present potential solutions as well...

Exactly. The lead talk should not be “here are seven ways graphs fail.” It should present a production architecture that addresses those failures.

A stronger formulation is:

> **The Graph Is Not the Factory: A Reference Architecture for Production Coding Agents**

The organizing pattern should be:

`failure → architectural control → proof that the control works`

For example:

1. **Retries duplicate external actions**

   Solution: durable intent records, stable idempotency keys, tool receipts, deduplication, and compensation paths.

   Proof: crash immediately after creating a branch or PR, resume the graph, and show that the external action occurs only once.

2. **Parallel agents create conflicting state and patches**

   Solution: isolated workspaces, typed state reducers, explicit artifact ownership, deterministic joins, and conflict escalation.

   Proof: run two agents against overlapping files and demonstrate safe merge, rejection, or human escalation.

3. **Approvals become stale**

   Solution: bind approval to the exact artifact hash, repository revision, policy version, proposed action, and expiry.

   Proof: change the repository after approval and show that execution fails closed rather than applying the stale decision.

4. **Graph replay is not reproducible**

   Solution: a run manifest pinning the graph, state schema, prompt, model, tool contract, policy, and evaluator versions.

   Proof: resume an old checkpoint after deploying a new graph and demonstrate controlled migration or quarantine.

5. **An allowed edge becomes an authorization bypass**

   Solution: per-node workload identity, least-privilege capabilities, trusted state labels, sandboxing, and action-scoped authorization.

   Proof: inject a manipulated tool description or credential-scope mismatch and show the policy layer denying it.

6. **Traces show activity but not correctness**

   Solution: connect execution traces to node, transition, trajectory, outcome, and policy evaluations.

   Proof: show a graph that completes successfully but fails its artifact or trajectory invariant.

7. **Fan-out destroys the economics**

   Solution: branch-level token, tool, retry, concurrency, and latency budgets with admission control and early termination.

   Proof: compare unrestricted fan-out with budgeted execution using quality, latency, and cost measurements.

For a 15–20 minute talk, I would not give all seven equal time. Use three failures as live or recorded demonstrations—duplicate side effects, conflicting parallel edits, and stale approval—then show how the seven controls fit into one reference architecture.

The audience should leave with three reusable artifacts:

- a production reference architecture;
- a failure-injection matrix;
- a run-manifest and evidence contract.

The proposal’s central promise becomes:

> I will take a plausible coding-agent graph, break it in production-relevant ways, then rebuild it with durability, side-effect safety, isolation, authorization, evaluation, budgets, and lifecycle controls. The result is a practical definition of what turns an agent graph into an AI software factory.

That is much more acceptance-worthy: it has a problem, an implementable solution, empirical proof, and something attendees can apply to their own systems.

> Also how does my threadloop project relate to this? and the governed agent autonomy patterns project?

I’m falling back to the two local checkouts and will cite their current files and commits directly; any relationship I describe will be an architectural synthesis, not a declared dependency unless the code shows one.

The two projects give the talk its solution architecture.

> **Governed Agent Autonomy Patterns governs execution inside a node or agent loop. ThreadLoop governs advancement across the software-delivery lifecycle.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    I["Issue and task intent"] --> T1["ThreadLoop: lifecycle authority"]
    T1 --> H["Governed harness: execution authority"]
    H --> S["Sandboxed tools and bounded mutations"]
    S --> V["Independent verification"]
    V --> R["Content-addressed run receipt"]
    R --> T2["ThreadLoop: receipt validation and staleness checks"]
    T2 --> Q["Review, repair, human approval, and completion"]
```

## How the projects divide responsibility

| Project | Primary question | Contribution to the talk |
|---|---|---|
| **Governed Agent Autonomy Patterns** | “May this agent action execute?” | Plan approval, permissions, capability trust, isolation, budgets, exact-subject approval, independent verification, and execution receipts |
| **ThreadLoop** | “May this task advance?” | Durable lifecycle state, optimistic concurrency, idempotent transitions, proof staleness, repair loops, signed CI/review evidence, human approval, completion authority, and audit history |
| **The missing integration** | “Can proof from the governed execution safely authorize the next lifecycle transition?” | The concrete system and experiment that would make the summit talk original |

## Governed Agent Autonomy Patterns: the governed node

This project is effectively the implementation of loop engineering.

The provider does not own execution authority. The repository-owned harness decides whether tools run, approvals are valid, lifecycle advances, verification passes, and success can be declared. [Harness architecture](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/examples/governed-coding-agent/README.md:3)

It already supplies several of the proposed solutions:

- exact-subject approvals bind the run, scope, digest and event position;
- capability changes invalidate earlier trust;
- token, tool-call and cost limits fail closed;
- protected actions require an approved plan;
- source mutations run through bounded repository tools and isolated containers;
- verification is performed against the exact workspace digest by an independent verifier;
- the final receipt contains approvals, usage, cost, patch/workspace digests, verification and cleanup evidence. [Enforced controls](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/examples/governed-coding-agent/README.md:39), [approval binding](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/examples/governed-coding-agent/src/harness.ts:312), [budget enforcement](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/examples/governed-coding-agent/src/harness.ts:626), [receipt construction](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/examples/governed-coding-agent/src/harness.ts:1197)

BoundaryBench adds the failure-first evaluation method: frozen decisions, unsafe mutants and reproducible evidence. That is the beginning of the talk’s experimental proof.

Its limitation is important: the harness currently creates its lifecycle and ledger in memory and assembles the receipt at the end of a trial. It is not yet a general crash-resumable, distributed graph runtime. The repository also explicitly says there are no live pilot results yet. [Run initialization](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/examples/governed-coding-agent/src/harness.ts:239), [claim boundary](~/Code/governed-agent-autonomy-patterns/README.md:80)

## ThreadLoop: the outer work graph

ThreadLoop is already a concrete answer to “graph topology is not enough.”

Its lifecycle is an explicit cyclic state graph:

`queued → framed → proof_ready → implementing → verifying → reviewing ↔ repairing → ready_for_human → completed`

But the edge alone never authorizes advancement. Each transition is guarded by plans, current-HEAD proof, repair budgets, review state, approval and merge observations. [Lifecycle graph](~/Code/threadloop/docs/lifecycle.md:3)

It contributes:

- persistent SQLite lifecycle state;
- expected state versions and idempotency keys;
- atomic transition, audit and idempotency records;
- immutable receipts that become stale after a new commit;
- bounded repair re-entry;
- signed, identity-bound CI and review evidence;
- same-HEAD human approval and merge requirements for completion;
- separation between lifecycle authority and telemetry. [Transition transaction](~/Code/threadloop/docs/lifecycle.md:51), [transition authorities](~/Code/threadloop/docs/lifecycle.md:56), [telemetry boundary](~/Code/threadloop/docs/observability.md:67)

ThreadLoop is therefore closer to a proof-carrying workflow controller than an agent framework. It does not decide how an agent reasons, dynamically schedule arbitrary graph nodes, or govern every tool action inside implementation. The caller executes work; ThreadLoop determines whether the resulting evidence authorizes advancement.

## The combined architecture

A credible integration would work like this:

1. ThreadLoop creates the immutable task and proof plan.
2. It authorizes entry into `implementing`.
3. The governed harness executes the coding run under the five gates.
4. The harness emits a receipt bound to the plan, capability set, budget, patch and workspace digest.
5. A signing adapter wraps that receipt with ThreadLoop’s session, gate, repository, branch and HEAD identities.
6. ThreadLoop imports and verifies it without automatically advancing state.
7. An explicit transition revalidates the current repository and evidence.
8. Independent review, repair and same-HEAD human approval remain outside the implementing agent’s authority.

There is no direct code dependency between the two local repositories today, and their receipt formats are not currently compatible. That is useful: the integration is a real research contribution, not something to imply already exists.

## How this strengthens the lead proposal

The talk becomes:

> **The Graph Is Not the Factory: Building Proof-Carrying Coding Agents with Governed Loops and Durable Lifecycles**

The practical case study can demonstrate:

- capability drift invalidated by the governed harness;
- stale code or approval rejected by ThreadLoop;
- budget exhaustion stopping execution without marking the task complete;
- independent verification producing a digest-bound receipt;
- a later review blocker forcing lifecycle re-entry into repair;
- exact receipt replay remaining idempotent;
- a crash during the inner harness exposing the remaining durability gap.

That last point matters. You are not presenting the projects as a finished AI factory. You are using two implemented systems to show what the factory requires, which controls already work, where their authority boundaries meet, and what remains unsolved.

Current evidence boundary: the governed-autonomy checkout is clean, but its own documentation limits the evidence to deterministic conformance rather than production outcomes. ThreadLoop’s local `issue-42/review-audit-handoff` checkout contains extensive uncommitted work, so the review-sensor and audit surfaces should be presented as working-tree implementation until they are separately committed, tested and landed. The Qodo codebase index returned no matches for either repository, so this assessment comes from the current local checkouts rather than indexed cross-repository analysis.

Draft:

I did a first architecture pass on the “graph engineering” idea, and I think there’s a strong CODE Summit proposal in it:

**The Graph Is Not the Factory: Building Proof-Carrying Coding Agents with Governed Loops and Durable Lifecycles**

Graph engineering gives us a way to compose multi-step agents: nodes, tools, branches, evaluators, and human gates. But the graph only describes the execution topology. It does not make an AI factory reliable.

At scale, the hard problems are durable state, safe retries, concurrent workspace changes, stale approvals, permission drift, budget enforcement, independent verification, and proving exactly what ran. The talk would pair each problem with an implementable control:

- Crashes and retries after side effects → durable intents, idempotency keys, and replay-safe receipts
- Code, policy, or tools changing after approval → approvals bound to the exact digest, repository HEAD, capabilities, and expiry
- The agent claiming its own work passed → independent verification and content-addressed evidence
- An agent run finishing before the task is safely complete → separate execution authority from lifecycle authority

That last distinction is where my two projects fit.

**Governed Agent Autonomy Patterns** governs the inner execution loop: planning, permissions, tool trust, budgets, isolation, and verification.

## Canonical Contracts

Wake input:

```text
repo_root: canonical dedicated worktree path
session_id: explicit ThreadLoop session
wake_id: stable scheduler delivery identity
mode: normal | replay
```

Transition key:

```text
runner:v1:<wake_id>:<expected_state_version>
```

Wake invariant:

1. Verify repository, branch, HEAD, cleanliness, session, and protocol v3.
2. Read `session next --json`.
3. If terminal or human-owned, stop.
4. If the candidate is executable, submit exactly that transition and stop.
5. Otherwise, perform at most one explicitly allowed `required_work` action and stop.
6. Unknown work codes fail closed.

A successful or replayed transition is always the final action of that wake. This proves idempotent transition delivery; it does not claim exactly-once agent execution.

## TDD And BDD Implementation Strategy

Vertical slices:

1. Exact duplicate transition → one state change and one audit event.
2. Lost-response retry → byte-identical replay with no new event.
3. Changed request under the same key → `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`.
4. Distinct concurrent wakes → one winner and one `STATE_VERSION_CONFLICT`.
5. SignalPay replay → implementation, review blocker, descendant repair, re-verification, then `ready_for_human`.
6. Unknown or human-owned work → stop without generic execution.

Tests should assert through `protocol`, `session next`, `session transition`, gate, review, and audit CLI projections—not SQLite internals.

## Component Design

The skill is the orchestration module. Existing ThreadLoop commands remain the interface and lifecycle authority. The external scheduler owns wake delivery and worktree serialization.

No `Runner` class, action-dispatch framework, scheduler interface, plugin registry, or lease abstraction belongs in `src/`.

## Failure And Recovery Rules

- Dirty or mismatched checkout: preserve it and stop; never clean/reset automatically.
- State-version conflict: stop; a later wake must reread state.
- Idempotency conflict: retain both request digests; never mint a replacement key in the same wake.
- Missing/stale/corrupt evidence: perform at most one declared recovery action.
- Repair budget exhausted: stop for explicit block evidence.
- `ready_for_human`, approval, merge, deployment, publication, secret rotation, or policy activation: stop.
- Crash after an ambiguous transition response: retry the identical request with the same `wake_id`.
- Crash during implementation: preserve the worktree; do not silently restart it.

- Config, draft, and manifest remain `v0.2.0`.
- Receipt remains `boundarybench.receipt.v0.1.0`.
- Store markers under `.boundarybench/runs/<run-set-id>/attempts/<run-id>.json`.
- Use exclusive creation and flush before admission succeeds.

## Canonical Contracts

Marker:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "boundarybench.attempt-start.v0.1.0",
  "runSetId": "<frozen run set>",
  "manifestDigest": "sha256:<digest>",
  "runId": "<exact frozen cell>",
  "taskId": "<task>",
  "provider": "<provider>",
  "condition": "<condition>",
  "startedAt": "<ISO timestamp>",
  "markerDigest": "sha256:<preceding fields>"
}
```

State derivation:

| Marker | Valid receipt | State | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Absent | Absent | `never_started` | Eligible for exclusive acquisition |
| Valid | Absent | `uncertain` | Stop before provider work |
| Valid | Present | `finalized` | Preserve and continue |
| Absent | Present | `legacy_finalized` | Preserve; never replay |
| Invalid/foreign | Any | `invalid` | Fail closed |

The experiment-local module exposes only `inspect()` and `begin()`. A terminal receipt remains completion evidence.

## TDD And BDD Implementation Strategy

Vertical slices:

1. Two simultaneous `begin` calls → exactly one `acquired`.
2. Start marker without receipt → `uncertain`, never pending.
3. Marker plus valid receipt → `finalized`.
4. Malformed, foreign, or digest-mismatched marker → fail before provider work.
5. Simulated provider activity followed by pre-receipt failure → restart makes zero provider calls.
6. Legacy valid receipt without marker → remains terminal.

## Component Design

`FileAttemptJournal` owns admission and classification. `runExperiment` owns sequencing. `GovernedHarness` still owns one attempt, and `AtomicEvidenceSink` still owns terminal publication.

The exclusive marker create is the admission transaction; the atomic receipt rename is completion. A crash between them is intentionally `uncertain`.

No storage adapter registry or generic `RunJournal` should be introduced.

## Failure And Recovery Rules

- Marker write/flush fails: no model construction or call.
- Existing marker without receipt: retain the run set and stop.
- Invalid or foreign marker: fail closed; do not repair or overwrite it.
- Two processes race: one acquires; every loser stops.
- Crash after marker but before provider work: conservatively uncertain.
- Crash during provider work: preserve unknown usage; never convert it to zero.
- Receipt write fails: retain marker and stop.
- Any uncertain attempt stops later cells because aggregate spend is unknown.
- Recovery requires investigation and, if another sample is authorized, a newly seeded and frozen run set.

2. `fix(experiment): stop resume on uncertain attempts`
3. `docs(experiment): define crash-visible resume semantics`

# ThreadLoop Consumer-Repository Feature Pilot Build Plan

## Summary

The next ThreadLoop acceptance target is a supervised, real consumer-repository feature run:

> Can Codex use the ThreadLoop runner skill while implementing a fresh feature in SignalPay, continue across separate wakes, preserve lifecycle and proof state, respond to current review evidence, and stop at `ready_for_human`?

The pilot needs the runner skill and the existing ThreadLoop CLI. It does **not** need `runner-replay.test.ts`, a controller extracted from that test, or a new scheduler product.

The role of each existing artifact is:

- `.agents/skills/threadloop-runner/SKILL.md`: the procedure Codex follows for one explicit wake.
- ThreadLoop CLI: lifecycle, proof, review, audit, and guarded-transition authority.
- `tests/integration/runner-replay.test.ts`: ThreadLoop-internal regression coverage only; it is not installed, copied, imported, or executed by SignalPay.
- The operator or a simple scheduled task: supplies the four wake inputs, retains the wake handoff, and starts the next Codex wake.
- The human: retains approval, merge, recovery, and policy authority.

This is intentionally a supervised pilot. A manually retained wake record and explicit invocations are sufficient to test whether the skill is usable. If the pilot later demonstrates that manual wake delivery is the dominant friction, that evidence can justify a separate controller or scheduler build.

Current state on 2026-07-30:

- ThreadLoop `origin/main` is `1312105dc860fe67c32eb207763fd262ff28282a`.
- The runner skill is on `feat/issue-43-runner-contract@dce6d423bd790258ec09f84e3115b38632da8d6d`.
- ThreadLoop PR #68 and issue #43 are closed, but the live consumer-repository pilot was not run.
- SignalPay `main` is `a6e832cd8a5e031a3ea65729e04f1406ccf59b88`.
- SignalPay PR #4 remains an open refund PR and is not the pilot target.
- The current SignalPay checkout contains unrelated untracked local artifacts, so the pilot must use a fresh worktree.

The intended review unit is the SignalPay pilot feature pull request. The runner skill must first be available from a reviewed, immutable ThreadLoop commit, but the pilot does not add ThreadLoop runtime code.

## Skills To Use

- `software-build-plan`: keep the consumer pilot implementation-ready and separate from future automation.
- `threadloop-runner`: govern each explicit Codex wake and enforce the one-action and human-authority boundaries.
- `tdd-bdd`: require failing SignalPay behavior tests before production code.
- `failure-path-testing`: prove idempotency, state-transition rejection, and no-mutation failure paths.
- `workflow-invariants`: verify the wake, lifecycle, evidence, and authority boundaries throughout the run.
- `dx-audit`: record setup burden, manual handoffs, unclear stops, and context-restart usability.
- `code-review`: perform the mandatory final Standards and Spec review against the SignalPay feature fixed point.

## Scope

### In scope

- Make the reviewed runner skill available in the fresh SignalPay worktree.
- Use an immutable ThreadLoop package and signer commit SHA.
- Create a dedicated SignalPay worktree and feature branch from current `origin/main`.
- Start one explicit ThreadLoop session for one bounded feature.
- Retain the four runner inputs and each wake result in a pilot handoff record.
- Invoke Codex separately for each wake using the runner skill.
- Have Codex write tests, implement one bounded feature, run focused checks, and create one scoped implementation commit when ThreadLoop authorizes `COMMIT_IMPLEMENTATION`.
- Run SignalPay’s immutable `make verify` gate through ThreadLoop.
- Collect and import current signed CI and review evidence outside the runner wake.
- Enter a bounded `COMMIT_REPAIR` wake only if the current review contains a legitimate blocking finding.
- Start at least one later wake in a fresh Codex context to test continuity without transcript memory.
- Stop at `ready_for_human` and export the verified audit trail.
- Record technical success and developer-experience friction.

The default fresh feature is **capture-state safety and retry semantics**:

- Only an `authorized` payment can begin a new capture.
- An exact idempotent retry of a successful capture returns the original response and emits no duplicate event.
- A new idempotency key against a `captured` or `pending` payment fails without mutation or a new event.
- Existing auth, scope, camelCase response, and event contracts remain stable.

### Out of scope

- Extracting any code from `runner-replay.test.ts`.
- Copying `runner-replay.test.ts` or a replay fixture into SignalPay.
- Making the historical SignalPay PR #4 replay the pilot result.
- Building a controller, scheduler, queue, lease service, agent launcher, provider abstraction, dashboard, or hosted service.
- Changing ThreadLoop lifecycle, schema, protocol, CLI, or runtime packages.
- Using the runner to push, open or merge a PR, approve, deploy, publish, rotate secrets, activate policy, or recover a blocked session.
- Manufacturing a review defect solely to force a repair cycle.
- Modifying, merging, or closing SignalPay PR #4.
- Same-checkout multi-agent execution.

## Package Layout / File-to-Task Mapping

### ThreadLoop source

- `.agents/skills/threadloop-runner/SKILL.md`: existing runner procedure copied or installed into SignalPay from the reviewed immutable ThreadLoop SHA.

- `.github/workflows/threadloop-review-sensor.yml`: existing reusable signed review sensor, pinned by the same full ThreadLoop commit SHA.

No ThreadLoop source file is added or extracted for this pilot.

### SignalPay pilot

- `.agents/skills/threadloop-runner/SKILL.md` **(new in the pilot worktree):** exact reviewed skill snapshot. Record its ThreadLoop source SHA in the file handoff or PR description.
- `.github/workflows/threadloop.yml` **(new):** minimal caller workflow for the pinned ThreadLoop gate and review sensors.
- `.threadloop/config.json` **(new):** visible repo-local ThreadLoop configuration. Commit it before the first runner wake.

The handoff record is an operating artifact, not a new controller or product schema. The operator can append it manually after each wake.

## Dependencies And Settings

- No new ThreadLoop runtime or development dependency.
- No SignalPay package dependency, database, or Node project metadata.
- Build the ThreadLoop CLI tarball from the reviewed full SHA and install it in a tool directory outside SignalPay, or invoke an already verified binary from that SHA.

- SignalPay’s immutable local gate is `make verify`.

  ```text

  session_id
  wake_id
  mode: normal
  ```

- Use one unique `wake_id` per scheduled delivery. Reuse it only for an ambiguous duplicate delivery of that same wake.
- Keep `.threadloop/state/`, receipt packages, wake handoffs, and the pilot report out of the feature diff unless explicitly selected as review evidence.

## Canonical Contracts

### Runner skill contract

Each Codex wake:

1. Receives the four explicit inputs.
2. Validates the canonical repository root, named branch, HEAD, clean worktree, protocol version, explicit session, audit status, and repair budget.
3. Reads `session next`.
4. Performs at most one authorized action:
   - one executable lifecycle transition;
   - one bounded `COMMIT_IMPLEMENTATION` or `COMMIT_REPAIR` action;
   - one stored local gate; or
   - no mutation and a handoff.
5. Stops after that action or handoff.

The skill is the runner. No extracted TypeScript controller sits between Codex and the existing ThreadLoop CLI in this pilot.

### Operator-retained wake handoff

Before a transition or other side effect, the operator retains the fields the skill requires:

```text
repo_root
session_id
wake_id
mode
branch
head_sha
worktree_clean
lifecycle_state
lifecycle_state_version
selected_action
action_started
action_outcome
action_result
transition_request
stop_reason
next_authority
```

The record may be maintained as one append-only local JSONL file. It is needed for honest duplicate/crash handling, but it does not require new runtime code.

### Coding-agent action

During `COMMIT_IMPLEMENTATION`, Codex may:

- Read the task, rules, and plan.
- Write failing behavior tests.
- Implement the smallest feature.
- Run focused non-ThreadLoop checks.
- Create at most one scoped commit.

It must leave a clean worktree and stop. It must not run a ThreadLoop gate, transition, evidence import, push, or PR action in the same wake.

`COMMIT_REPAIR` follows the same boundary and is limited to the complete current blocking finding set.

### External evidence handoff

The runner stops when signed CI or review evidence is required. The operator:

1. Invokes the exact pinned caller workflow.
2. Downloads the exact package for the current feature HEAD.
3. Imports it using the explicit session.
4. Records the result in the wake handoff.
5. Starts a later wake with a new `wake_id`.

These are supervised pilot operations, not runner behavior.

### Human stop

At `ready_for_human`, `blocked`, `completed`, or exhausted repair budget, Codex starts no new action. The pilot ends at `ready_for_human` without approval or merge.

## TDD And BDD Implementation Strategy

The feature wake begins with these red scenarios:

1. Authorized payment + new key -> one capture and one event.
2. Same key retry -> identical response and no second event.
3. Captured payment + new key -> conflict, no mutation, no event.
4. Pending payment + new key -> conflict, no mutation, no event.
5. Missing scope or idempotency key -> existing fail-closed behavior remains.

Only after the targeted tests demonstrate the gap does Codex modify `src/signalpay_api/app.py`. It then reruns the focused tests and creates one feature commit.

Full `make verify` is not bundled into the implementation action. ThreadLoop runs it later as the stored local gate while the repository is clean and committed.

If review produces a legitimate blocker, a later repair wake begins from a test or reproduction for that finding, applies the smallest correction, and creates one repair commit. All local and signed evidence must then be refreshed for the repair HEAD.

The pilot deliberately starts at least one verification, review, or repair wake in a fresh Codex context. The new context receives only the repository, the runner skill, and the four explicit inputs.

## Component Design

The pilot uses the existing architecture:

```text
operator or scheduled task
  -> four explicit wake inputs
  -> Codex reads runner skill
  -> existing ThreadLoop CLI projection
  -> one Codex action or one handoff
  -> operator records outcome
  -> later independent wake
```

ThreadLoop owns lifecycle truth, proof plans, receipts, review evidence, repair budget, guarded transitions, and audit persistence.

The runner skill owns the procedure for one wake. Codex owns the bounded code change. The operator owns wake delivery and the local handoff record. GitHub Actions owns signed sensor execution. The human owns irreversible authority.

The pilot is testing whether this division is usable. Adding a software controller before running the pilot would hide the coordination friction the experiment needs to reveal.

## Failure And Recovery Rules

- Missing or invalid wake input -> run no ThreadLoop command; operator corrects the invocation.
- Dirty worktree before a wake -> preserve it exactly and stop; never clean, reset, stash, or repeat work automatically.
- Branch, HEAD, repository, session, or protocol mismatch -> stop and record the observed facts.
- Ambiguous transition response -> reuse the same wake ID and exact retained request only after revalidating the Git snapshot.
- `STATE_VERSION_CONFLICT` or `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT` -> stop; do not mint a new key in the same wake.
- Crash during repository work -> preserve the worktree and mark the handoff outcome unknown; a human inspects before any later action.
- Uncertain local gate outcome -> do not replay it as a duplicate.
- Missing, stale, or corrupt proof -> remain in the current state and follow the exact required-work handoff.
- Signed package collection/import failure -> retain the current lifecycle state and exact error; retry only under operator supervision.
- Blocking review finding -> enter repair only through the executable reviewing-to-repairing transition and within budget.
- Clean review -> do not invent a defect to exercise repair.
- Fresh Codex context cannot continue -> record a failed usability criterion; do not compensate with hidden transcript context.
- Unknown required-work code -> fail closed and hand it to the operator.
- `ready_for_human`, blocked state, exhausted budget, approval, or merge requirement -> stop for human authority.

## Commit Plan

### ThreadLoop skill prerequisite

1. `feat(runner): add one-action wake contract and transition proof`
   - Review the existing branch’s skill and its small ThreadLoop regression test together.
   - The test remains internal and is not promoted to pilot code.
2. `docs(runner): document supervised consumer pilot boundary`

If those commits are not merged before the pilot, pin the exact reviewed `dce6d423bd790258ec09f84e3115b38632da8d6d` snapshot and describe the pilot as pre-merge validation.

1. Review the exact ThreadLoop runner-skill branch against current `origin/main`.
2. Either merge a new/reopened runner-skill PR or explicitly pin the reviewed branch SHA for a pre-merge pilot. Do not imply the closed PR is merged.

- compound-engineering:docs:ankane-readme-writer: Creates or updates README files following Ankane-style template for Ruby gems. Use when writing gem documentation with imperative voice, concise prose, and standard section ordering. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:research:best-practices-researcher: Researches and synthesizes external best practices, documentation, and examples for any technology or framework. Use when you need industry standards, community conventions, or implementation guidance. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:research:framework-docs-researcher: Gathers comprehensive documentation and best practices for frameworks, libraries, or dependencies. Use when you need official docs, version-specific constraints, or implementation patterns. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:research:git-history-analyzer: Performs archaeological analysis of git history to trace code evolution, identify contributors, and understand why code patterns exist. Use when you need historical context for code changes. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:research:learnings-researcher: Searches docs/solutions/ for relevant past solutions by frontmatter metadata. Use before implementing features or fixing problems to surface institutional knowledge and prevent repeated mistakes. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:research:repo-research-analyst: Conducts thorough research on repository structure, documentation, conventions, and implementation patterns. Use when onboarding to a new codebase or understanding project conventions. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:agent-native-reviewer: Reviews code to ensure agent-native parity — any action a user can take, an agent can also take. Use after adding UI features, agent tools, or system prompts. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:architecture-strategist: Analyzes code changes from an architectural perspective for pattern compliance and design integrity. Use when reviewing PRs, adding services, or evaluating structural refactors. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:code-simplicity-reviewer: Final review pass to ensure code is as simple and minimal as possible. Use after implementation is complete to identify YAGNI violations and simplification opportunities. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:data-integrity-guardian: Reviews database migrations, data models, and persistent data code for safety. Use when checking migration safety, data constraints, transaction boundaries, or privacy compliance. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:data-migration-expert: Validates data migrations, backfills, and production data transformations against reality. Use when PRs involve ID mappings, column renames, enum conversions, or schema changes. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:deployment-verification-agent: Produces Go/No-Go deployment checklists with SQL verification queries, rollback procedures, and monitoring plans. Use when PRs touch production data, migrations, or risky data changes. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:dhh-rails-reviewer: Brutally honest Rails code review from DHH's perspective. Use when reviewing Rails code for anti-patterns, JS framework contamination, or violations of Rails conventions. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:julik-frontend-races-reviewer: Reviews JavaScript and Stimulus code for race conditions, timing issues, and DOM lifecycle problems. Use after implementing or modifying frontend controllers or async UI code. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:kieran-python-reviewer: Reviews Python code with an extremely high quality bar for Pythonic patterns, type safety, and maintainability. Use after implementing features, modifying code, or creating new Python modules. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:kieran-rails-reviewer: Reviews Rails code with an extremely high quality bar for conventions, clarity, and maintainability. Use after implementing features, modifying code, or creating new Rails components. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:kieran-typescript-reviewer: Reviews TypeScript code with an extremely high quality bar for type safety, modern patterns, and maintainability. Use after implementing features, modifying code, or creating new TypeScript components. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:pattern-recognition-specialist: Analyzes code for design patterns, anti-patterns, naming conventions, and duplication. Use when checking codebase consistency or verifying new code follows established patterns. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:performance-oracle: Analyzes code for performance bottlenecks, algorithmic complexity, database queries, memory usage, and scalability. Use after implementing features or when performance concerns arise. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:schema-drift-detector: Detects unrelated schema.rb changes in PRs by cross-referencing against included migrations. Use when reviewing PRs with database schema changes. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:review:security-sentinel: Performs security audits for vulnerabilities, input validation, auth/authz, hardcoded secrets, and OWASP compliance. Use when reviewing code for security issues or before deployment. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:workflow:bug-reproduction-validator: Systematically reproduces and validates bug reports to confirm whether reported behavior is an actual bug. Use when you receive a bug report or issue that needs verification. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:workflow:every-style-editor: Reviews and edits text content to conform to Every's editorial style guide. Use when written content needs style compliance checks for headlines, punctuation, voice, and formatting. (Tools: Task, Glob, Grep, LS, ExitPlanMode, Read, Edit, MultiEdit, Write, NotebookRead, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch)
- compound-engineering:workflow:lint: Use this agent when you need to run linting and code quality checks on Ruby and ERB files. Run before pushing to origin. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:workflow:pr-comment-resolver: Addresses PR review comments by implementing requested changes and reporting resolutions. Use when code review feedback needs to be resolved with code changes. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:workflow:spec-flow-analyzer: Analyzes specifications and feature descriptions for user flow completeness and gap identification. Use when a spec, plan, or feature description needs flow analysis, edge case discovery, or requirements validation. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- gsd-codebase-mapper: Explores codebase and writes structured analysis documents. Spawned by map-codebase with a focus area (tech, arch, quality, concerns). Writes documents directly to reduce orchestrator context load. (Tools: Read, Bash, Grep, Glob, Write)
- gsd-debugger: Investigates bugs using scientific method, manages debug sessions, handles checkpoints. Spawned by /gsd:debug orchestrator. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebSearch)

- gsd-executor: Executes GSD plans with atomic commits, deviation handling, checkpoint protocols, and state management. Spawned by execute-phase orchestrator or execute-plan command. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)
- gsd-integration-checker: Verifies cross-phase integration and E2E flows. Checks that phases connect properly and user workflows complete end-to-end. (Tools: Read, Bash, Grep, Glob)

- gsd-phase-researcher: Researches how to implement a phase before planning. Produces RESEARCH.md consumed by gsd-planner. Spawned by /gsd:plan-phase orchestrator. (Tools: Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch, mcp__context7__*)
- gsd-plan-checker: Verifies plans will achieve phase goal before execution. Goal-backward analysis of plan quality. Spawned by /gsd:plan-phase orchestrator. (Tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep)

- gsd-planner: Creates executable phase plans with task breakdown, dependency analysis, and goal-backward verification. Spawned by /gsd:plan-phase orchestrator. (Tools: Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, mcp__context7__*)

- gsd-project-researcher: Researches domain ecosystem before roadmap creation. Produces files in .planning/research/ consumed during roadmap creation. Spawned by /gsd:new-project or /gsd:new-milestone orchestrators. (Tools: Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch, mcp__context7__*)
- gsd-research-synthesizer: Synthesizes research outputs from parallel researcher agents into SUMMARY.md. Spawned by /gsd:new-project after 4 researcher agents complete. (Tools: Read, Write, Bash)

- gsd-roadmapper: Creates project roadmaps with phase breakdown, requirement mapping, success criteria derivation, and coverage validation. Spawned by /gsd:new-project orchestrator. (Tools: Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep)

- gsd-verifier: Verifies phase goal achievement through goal-backward analysis. Checks codebase delivers what phase promised, not just that tasks completed. Creates VERIFICATION.md report. (Tools: Read, Bash, Grep, Glob)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md

## claude.ai Gamma
Gamma creates AI-powered presentations, documents, webpages, and social posts. Only include optional parameters when the user explicitly requests or clearly implies them. Gamma has intelligent defaults - when in doubt, omit. When uncertain about user preferences, ask rather than assume. The read_gamma tool can read the content of an existing Gamma when given its file ID. Existing gammas have a type: "template" or "regular". Only templates can be used with generate_from_template; use get_gammas with type="template" to discover valid templates. Non-template IDs are not valid inputs to generate_from_template. If generate_from_template reports that an ID is inaccessible or not a template, find a valid template with get_gammas(type="template"). If the user's intent is to create a new gamma, but not by using an existing template, then use the generate tool. IMPORTANT: The tools provided by this server cannot edit or modify existing gammas. Do not suggest that you can make changes, adjustments, or refinements to a generated gamma. Instead, let the user know they can customize their gamma directly in the Gamma editor.

## plugin:compound-engineering:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- agent-browser: Automates browser interactions for web testing, form filling, screenshots, and data extraction. Use when the user needs to navigate websites, interact with web pages, fill forms, take screenshots, test web applications, or extract information from web pages.
- code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/PRD asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".
- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- dx-audit: This skill should be used after modifying any code that forms part of the developer interface of a project — including CLI commands, public APIs, error handling, logging, setup scripts, or module structure. Audits Developer Experience across eight dimensions grouped into surface DX (CLI ergonomics, error handling, setup friction, output/feedback) and code DX (API ergonomics, debugging/observability, testability, extensibility). Produces a prioritized report of findings. Does not modify code.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- pythonic: Review Python code for Pythonic idioms, best practices, and readability. Use when checking Python code quality or when the user asks about making code more Pythonic.
- qa: Interactive QA session where user reports bugs or issues conversationally, and the agent files GitHub issues. Explores the codebase in the background for context and domain language. Use when user wants to report bugs, do QA, file issues conversationally, or mentions "QA session".
- qodo-codebase-wisdom: Understand how code works, how a change was done before, and which repos are coupled — to answer a question, plan a code change, debug a regression, or scope a fix, using the qodo CLI's managed tools. Use when a task needs to understand a codebase, its history, or how its repos relate — especially for a repo you don't have checked out or work spanning repos — "how does X work", "where is X defined", "who changed X", "explain this service", "plan the change for X", "what would changing X affect", "which repos depend on X", "why did X regress / when did it break", "has this been fixed before", "how did we solve X". - When a task needs knowledge about code, its change history, or cross-repo coupling — answering, planning a code change, debugging a regression, or scoping a fix — especially for repos not checked out locally or work spanning repos. Skip it for local-only work in a repo you already have checked out where reading the working tree answers it, and for non-code product/UX planning. It reads and cites; it never edits code or posts to the forge.
- qodo-get-rules: Load the coding rules from Qodo most relevant to the current coding task, using the qodo CLI's managed rules search — generate structured semantic queries from the assignment, retrieve the workspace's matching rules ranked by relevance, and apply them while writing the code. Use when the user asks to write, edit, refactor, or review code, when starting implementation planning, or on "get rules", "load qodo rules", "fetch coding rules", "relevant rules", "search rules". Skip if rules are already loaded in this conversation. - Before writing, editing, refactoring, or reviewing code in a workspace that has Qodo configured — the retrieved rules constrain the code you are about to produce. Skip when "Qodo Rules Loaded" already appears earlier in the conversation (don't re-fetch), and for tasks that produce no code (pure research, product questions).
- qodo-review: Review your LOCAL changes before opening a pull request, using the qodo CLI — send your uncommitted/unpushed diff to Qodo's review engine along with the coding-session context (what you changed and why, plus links to the ticket/spec/design that drove it) that a forge-based reviewer can never see, then evaluate the findings and apply the fixes you approve (or pass `autofix` to apply directly). Use when asked to "review my changes before I push", "pre-PR review", "check this before I open a PR", "review my local diff", or "run qodo review". - When the user wants a code review of local changes BEFORE any pull request exists — the pre-PR complement to resolving a PR's review findings. It sends the local diff plus your coding-session context (you just wrote this code — you're the only reviewer input that knows why) through qodo's managed review agent and returns structured findings; fixing them is your normal editing work. Skip it once a PR is open (resolve the PR's review instead), and for non-review chores (committing, pushing, opening the PR).
- qodo-review-resolver: Read or resolve a pull request's Qodo review with the qodo CLI. Fetch the structured review — status, the reviewed commit SHA, and every finding with its status — for ANY PR (yours or someone else's) as JSON, then optionally resolve the open findings in code, once or in a watch loop until it comes back clean. Use this — never `gh`/`curl` scraping of the PR's review comments — whenever you need to know where a review stands or what it flagged: "is the review clean on PR #N", "get Qodo's findings for <pr> as JSON", "what did Qodo flag on that PR", "is this PR's review up to date with head", "check the review before merging", plus "resolve my PR review", "fix the review findings", "address Qodo's findings", "babysit / watch this PR until it's clean". - When you need to read or act on a pull request's Qodo review — check where it stands, see what it flagged, gate a merge on it being clean at head, or fix the open findings — for any PR, not just your own. It reads the review through qodo's managed tool (structured, git-provider-agnostic), so use it instead of scraping the rendered PR review comments with `gh`/`curl` (lossy, provider-specific, and easy to read stale against the head commit). It never posts to the git forge — editing local code to resolve a finding is your normal work. Skip it for reviewing code you're writing locally before any PR exists (that's the pre-PR review), and for non-review PR chores (merging, labels, descriptions).
- qodo-setup: Authenticate with Qodo platform via browser-based OIDC login. Use when the user wants to set up Qodo, log in, or when another Qodo skill (like qodo-get-rules or qodo-pr-resolver) fails because no authentication is configured. Saves JWT to ~/.qodo/skill_auth.json for use by other Qodo skills.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- resolving-merge-conflicts: Use when you need to resolve an in-progress git merge/rebase conflict.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.

# Voice Canon

This skill is for voice fidelity and strategic clarity. It should make the work sound like a technical operator with a point of view, not a generic AI content system.

## Required Reading

1. Read `references/routing.md` first.
2. Read only the canon files required for the task type.
3. If the user provides source material, artifact links, repo findings, notes, or drafts, treat those as the factual source of truth. Use the canon for voice, framing, structure, and judgment.
4. If a public-facing claim depends on current names, dates, benchmark numbers, product behavior, laws, prices, or live publication state, verify it before presenting it as fact. If verification is not possible in the current context, label it as an unverified draft claim or remove it.

## Core Spine

Preserve this argument across substantial work:

- AI-assisted development increases output, but makes code integrity, review, and judgment more important.
- Speed is not the enemy. Unexamined speed is.
- Review is a responsibility boundary, not a bottleneck.
- Governance is not bureaucracy. It is how quality, accountability, and trust survive scale.
- Developer trust and executive confidence both matter. Durable adoption needs both.
- Tools should amplify human judgment, not replace ownership.
- Real systems, real tradeoffs, and visible proof are stronger than polished claims.

## Modes

Infer the mode from the user's request. If the request is ambiguous, choose the smallest mode that satisfies the user.

### `draft`

Create a new artifact from notes, a thesis, a repo finding, a content idea, or a target platform.

Use this sequence:

1. Identify the audience, artifact type, platform, and desired length.
2. Choose one core thesis, one content shape, and one enemy narrative.
3. Draft with concrete claims, real constraints, and a clear point of view.
4. Keep the piece focused on one job: curiosity, reproduction, adoption, trust, or executive translation.

### `rewrite`

Rewrite an existing draft while preserving facts, intent, and useful personality.

Default behavior:

- Return the rewritten version first.
- Then list the meaningful changes in a short note.
- Preserve natural spoken cadence, including short fragments and firm statements, when they strengthen the voice.
- Do not over-polish the draft into generic thought leadership.

### `critique`

Evaluate a draft, script, post, talk, or strategy.

Lead with the highest-impact issues:

- voice drift
- weak thesis
- generic AI commentary
- unsupported claims
- product-tour framing
- unclear audience
- missing evidence
- mixed funnel stages
- overexplaining

Then give specific fixes or a rewritten section.

### `strategy`

Plan a content angle, series, launch narrative, talk, workshop, field-enablement asset, or technical POV.

Anchor the strategy in:

- audience and adoption stage
- one core thesis
- one trust layer
- one proof source or evidence gap
- the next asset the reader, viewer, developer, or leader should want

### `repurpose`

Turn one strong idea, demo, recording, draft, or finding into multiple formats.

Guardrail: repurposing is only useful when the source idea has signal. If there is no clear thesis, evidence, audience, or learning, fix that before creating variants.

Each variant should add format-specific value. Do not make near-duplicate versions with different headings.

### `script`

Create teleprompter-ready or recording-ready narration.

Use natural spoken rhythm:

- short paragraphs
- clear turns
- concrete transitions
- minimal stage directions
- no stiff presenter language
- no broad setup before the point

When the user asks for exact wording, provide word-for-word copy.

### `demo-narrative`

Turn a technical run, repo finding, Qodo review, PR, screenshot, workshop moment, or field signal into a credible story.

Use this structure:

1. What was evaluated.
2. What looked fine or interesting at first.
3. What the tool, code, or workflow surfaced.
4. How a responsible engineer would interpret it.
5. What it proves, and what it does not prove.
6. Why it matters for trust, review, governance, or adoption.

Do not overclaim. For Qodo, agent, review, rules, or skills evidence, claim only what the visible source artifact proves.

## Voice Rules

Write with calm conviction:

- direct
- concrete
- systems-aware
- technically grounded
- governance-forward
- skeptical of hype
- respectful of serious engineering work
- willing to challenge weak narratives

Prefer:

- first person when the piece is personal, observational, or opinionated
- specific contrasts over broad slogans
- evidence, consequences, and tradeoffs over vibes
- real workflows, repos, review boundaries, and adoption friction over abstract trend commentary

- canned binary corrections such as "The question isn't X. It's Y.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "This is not X. It is Y.", and "It's not X. It's Y." State the claim directly instead; these formulas are not allowed in Nnenna's voice.
- generic AI optimism

- fear-mongering
- sarcasm or dunking

- inflated conclusions like "the future is bright" or "only time will tell"
- chatbot phrasing such as "great question", "let's dive in", or "I hope this helps"

## Output Checks

Before finalizing any substantive output, confirm internally:

- There is one clear thesis.
- The audience and artifact type are obvious.
- The piece uses a fitting content shape.
- It pushes back against a specific weak narrative or replaces it with a stronger frame.
- Public facts are verified, removed, or labeled as unverified draft claims.
- The language is direct, concrete, and not over-polished.
- The final text preserves judgment, trust, code integrity, governance, field enablement, or adoption infrastructure as the spine.

If the user's request is simple, do the work directly. Do not expose all of this scaffolding unless it helps the user evaluate the output.

## Core Thesis

**AI-assisted development has dramatically increased the amount of code we can produce, but it has made code integrity, review, and judgment the defining technical responsibility of this era.**

In other words:

Speed is abundant.  
Integrity is scarce.  
Judgment is the bottleneck.

## Sub-Theses

### 1. Code Review Is No Longer a Bottleneck. It Is a Boundary.

AI shifted where responsibility enters the system.

When humans stop writing every line of code, review becomes the moment where:

- Judgment re-enters
- Accountability is reclaimed
- Risk is surfaced instead of hidden

Treating review as friction is a category error. It is a safety boundary, not a slowdown.

Use this sub-thesis when writing about AI code review tools, developer workflow design, shift-left conversations, quality gates, and automation.

### 2. AI Did Not Reduce the Need for Meticulousness. It Raised the Cost of Its Absence.

Meticulousness is not personality. It is survival.

AI increases:

- Code volume
- Abstraction layers
- Hidden coupling
- Cognitive distance from execution

The less humans touch the code, the more precision matters.

Carelessness does not scale. It compounds.

Use this when addressing vibe coding culture, trust-the-model narratives, junior developer enablement, and claims that AI makes understanding optional.

### 3. Speed Without Integrity Is Just Technical Debt With Better Marketing.

AI makes it easy to confuse movement with progress.

Shipping fast feels good. Maintaining fast feels expensive.

Systems fail not because teams moved slowly, but because they moved fast without discipline.

This is how security incidents emerge, systems become brittle, and teams lose credibility over time.

Use this for incident analysis, postmortems, security conversations, and enterprise skepticism of AI hype.

### 4. Open Source Is Not Lower Stakes. It Is Shared Infrastructure.

Modern software runs on open source whether companies acknowledge it or not.

That means:

- The same rigor applies
- The same responsibility applies
- The blast radius is often larger, not smaller

AI-generated code does not become safer because it lives in OSS.

Use this when discussing OSS maintenance, supply chain security, enterprise dependency on OSS, and responsibility beyond ownership.

### 5. Judgment Is the Scarce Resource in AI-Assisted Development.

AI optimized generation. It did not optimize discernment.

The most valuable engineers are not the fastest typists or prompt writers. They are the ones who can:

- Evaluate tradeoffs
- Spot risk
- Ask the right questions
- Defend decisions under scrutiny

Use this when writing about senior engineering value, career growth, AI-replacing-developers narratives, and human-in-the-loop systems.

### 6. Code Integrity Is a Business Problem, Not Just a Technical One.

Poor code quality does not stay in engineering.

- Slower teams
- Higher incident costs
- Reputational damage
- Regulatory exposure
- Lost trust

### 7. The Industry Is Underestimating Risk Because It Is Inconvenient, Not Because It Is Small.

The industry prefers:

- Demos over durability
- Benchmarks over behavior
- Velocity over verifiability

Use this when challenging narratives, calling out shallow takes, writing high-risk/high-reward content, and positioning against trend cycles.

## Category Expansion: From Code Integrity to Adoption Infrastructure

### 8. AI Developer Tools Do Not Fail Because the Demo Is Bad. They Fail Because Adoption Is Under-Designed.

Use this when writing about AI developer tools, enterprise adoption, field enablement, strategic account education, and developer workflow change.

### 9. Developer Trust Is Enterprise Infrastructure.

Use this when writing about Developer Relations, community, open source, technical education, and AI tool adoption.

Use this when writing about the future of DevRel, Field CTO pathways, technical GTM, community-led adoption, and enterprise AI strategy.

Use this when writing about AI adoption strategy, developer experience, engineering leadership, change management, and enterprise rollout.

name: threadloop-runner
description:
  Run one fail-closed ThreadLoop v4 action for an explicitly identified scheduled wake in a dedicated Git worktree. Use
  when a scheduler delivers an explicit repo_root, session_id, wake_id, and mode and exactly one serialized wake must
  run - to run a scheduler wake, advance or step a ThreadLoop session, apply one ThreadLoop lifecycle transition, run
  one ThreadLoop gate, or execute one queued ThreadLoop task in its own worktree.
---

# ThreadLoop Runner

Use this skill for one serialized scheduler wake. ThreadLoop owns lifecycle state, guards, proof, review evidence, and
the repair budget. The scheduler owns wake uniqueness, serialization, and assignment of one dedicated worktree.

A wake may do exactly one of these:

- apply one executable ThreadLoop transition;
- perform one bounded repository action named by `required_work`;
- run one local gate named by the validated projection; or
- stop without mutation and hand off.

After any transition, repository action, or gate action, stop. Do not select a second action from the result.

## Required inputs

Require exactly these four explicit inputs:

- `repo_root`: canonical absolute path of the dedicated Git worktree;
- `session_id`: exact non-empty ThreadLoop session id;
- `wake_id`: 1-64 characters matching `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$`; and
- `mode`: exactly `normal` or `replay`.

Reject leading or trailing whitespace and NUL or newline characters. Do not infer an input from `PWD`, environment
variables, a prior wake, the current branch, or `threadloop session list`.

Both modes select at most one fresh action from a validated snapshot. `replay` records scheduler intent; it does not
select a fixture, package, sensor, or evidence source. Mode does not change lifecycle authority.

## Scheduler-retained wake record

Before an action starts, the scheduler must retain one record keyed by exact `(repo_root, session_id, wake_id)`. This
record is external to ThreadLoop and does not add a fifth runner input. Retain every field in
[references/wake-record.md](references/wake-record.md).

For a transition, retain the exact source, target, expected version, actor, input JSON bytes, and idempotency key. Write
the selected action and request before marking `action_started: true`. Scheduler serialization must prevent two
deliveries from both observing an absent record. If a duplicate delivery lacks a complete record, stop.

## Authority boundary

Never push, force-push, create a pull request, approve, merge, deploy, publish, rotate secrets, activate or replace
policy, or recover a blocked session. Never switch branches, rebase, reset, clean, stash, discard changes, or create or
delete a worktree.

One explicit ThreadLoop session must remain bound to one dedicated worktree. Only the scheduler can establish and
serialize that assignment.
