# Governed lifecycle

ThreadLoop stores lifecycle state on the task. A session remains the execution record attached to that task.

The ordered states are:

```text
queued
framed
proof_ready
implementing
verifying
pre_pr_reviewing
reviewing
repairing
ready_for_human
blocked
completed
```

The structural forward transitions are:

```text
queued -> framed
framed -> proof_ready
proof_ready -> implementing
implementing -> verifying
pre-PR verifying -> implementing | pre_pr_reviewing
pre_pr_reviewing -> implementing | reviewing
post-PR verifying -> reviewing | repairing
reviewing -> repairing | ready_for_human
repairing -> verifying
ready_for_human -> completed
```

Every state except `blocked` and `completed` may transition to `blocked`. Recovery from `blocked` may return only to the
recorded prior state, and `completed` is terminal.

Structural permission is not evidence that a transition should occur. Proof plans, gate receipts, review state, attempt
budgets, approval, and merge observations are separate guards layered onto this graph.

Lifecycle phase is derived from append-only transition history plus the immutable audit-genesis state that bounds
migrated history. A session is `pre_pr` until its first applied transition into `reviewing`; a migrated session whose
audit coverage begins in `reviewing`, `ready_for_human`, or `completed` is already `post_pr`. A legacy `repairing` state
or repair transition without evidence of entry into `reviewing` remains `pre_pr`, because older lifecycles allowed
pre-PR repair. The phase is permanently `post_pr` afterward. SQLite schema version 7 retains all prior lifecycle, proof,
signed receipt, audit, and repair records and adds this semantic interpretation without a second mutable phase flag.
Persistent triggers reject update, delete, and replacement. Repair usage remains derived from applied transitions into
`repairing`; historical entries remain counted, while new entries are allowed only for post-PR gate and signed-review
repairs.

`threadloop session next --session <id> --json` is read-only and returns one deterministic candidate or `null`. It
reports live Git facts without refreshing persisted snapshots. It rehashes the latest receipt manifest and output
artifacts, classifies local proof as missing/current/stale/failed/corrupt, and reports independent CI proof as
policy-missing/missing/passed/stale/corrupt. It also reports the three-cycle repair budget. Reading schema v2 or v3
reports proof migration without writing newer objects. Contract v4 also reports lifecycle phase and schema status,
pre-PR review evidence, the exact implementation basis, lifecycle history, current signed-review findings and
approval/merge state, audit validity/root/coverage, and one next human action. Reading schema v6 returns
`migration_required` without mutation; run `threadloop init` outside the runner to perform the transactional v7
migration.

`threadloop session transition` requires the caller's expected state version and an idempotency key. State mutation,
transition history, idempotency outcome, audit guard decision, active projection, and session completion are one
transaction. Accepted transitions append `transition_applied` in that same transaction. Exact replays add no duplicate
events, while rejected guards retain the unchanged lifecycle and one idempotent `guard_decision`.

| Transition                             | Required authority                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `framed -> proof_ready`                | Valid immutable plan plus clean named branch and baseline HEAD                                      |
| `proof_ready -> implementing`          | Repository still matches the plan baseline                                                          |
| `implementing -> verifying`            | One clean descendant commit after the current implementation basis                                  |
| pre-PR `verifying -> implementing`     | Current failed local proof or current-HEAD changes-required pre-PR review evidence                  |
| pre-PR `verifying -> pre_pr_reviewing` | Current local and signed CI proof for every gate on the clean plan branch                           |
| `pre_pr_reviewing -> implementing`     | Current-HEAD changes-required pre-PR review evidence                                                |
| `pre_pr_reviewing -> reviewing`        | Current-HEAD clean pre-PR review outcome plus current local and signed CI proof                     |
| post-PR `verifying -> repairing`       | Current-HEAD failure and fewer than three repair entries                                            |
| post-PR `verifying -> reviewing`       | Current local and signed CI proof                                                                   |
| `repairing -> verifying`               | Clean committed repair after the failure or signed-review basis                                     |
| `reviewing -> repairing`               | Current signed changes request or any unresolved, non-outdated signed-review thread                 |
| `reviewing -> ready_for_human`         | Current verified signed-review evidence without blockers                                            |

I read the local state before responding, and it's moved materially past what that transcript says. Then I found the thesis — written in your own repo.

## First, the state correction

| | Transcript said | Actually true now |
|---|---|---|
| ThreadLoop `main` | `1312105` | `6a59de9` (+4 PRs: #70, #72, #74, #76) |
| Runner skill | on a closed, unmerged PR #68 branch | **landed on `main`** at `.agents/skills/threadloop-runner/SKILL.md` + `references/wake-record.md`, `references/handoff.md` |
| Protocol / schema | v3 / SQLite 6 | **v4 / SQLite 7**, with a new `pre_pr_reviewing` state |
| ThreadLoop open work | #43 pilot, PR #68 | **one issue: #46, an esbuild dep bump.** No open PRs. Clean tree. |
| Governed | `6316a77` | `6316a77` — unchanged. Attempt-admission not built. |
| SignalPay pilot | planned | **not run.** No `.threadloop/`, no runner skill, no session. |

The thing to notice: **ThreadLoop's backlog is empty and neither project has ever produced a live run.** The planning loop from that conversation consumed its own runway. Every architectural question got answered; zero empirical ones did. Today is July 30 — Sept 15 early review is 6.5 weeks out.

## Second, the thesis is stronger than the one you were given

`docs/lifecycle.md:36` says this, in your own words:

> Structural permission is not evidence that a transition should occur. Proof plans, gate receipts, review state, attempt budgets, approval, and merge observations are separate guards layered onto this graph.

That's a sharper claim than "the graph is not the factory," which is a negation — reviewers see negations as category commentary. What you actually built is a positive mechanism. Read the authority table at `docs/lifecycle.md:60`: the word *current* appears in nearly every row. Current-HEAD proof. Current signed CI. Current-HEAD review evidence. Clean descendant commit after the current basis.

So the claim is:

> **In a production coding-agent graph, an edge is not a transition. It's an admission decision over evidence that expires.** Graph runtimes model edges as control flow and checkpoints as durable truth. Neither has a concept of *stale*. Software delivery is made almost entirely of evidence that goes stale the moment someone pushes a commit.

That answers Itamar's "graph engineering isn't enough" with a mechanism instead of a list of seven gaps. It's falsifiable in one demo: approve, then push, then watch the edge fail closed.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The reason ThreadLoop reads as graph engineering rather than a state machine is that its guards are **predicates over the external world**, not over internal state. `reviewing -> ready_for_human` doesn't ask "did review happen?" — it asks "is signed review evidence *currently* valid against *this* HEAD?" That inverts the usual durability story: LangGraph's checkpoint problem is *how do I resume without re-running side effects*; yours is *how do I refuse to resume when the world moved under the checkpoint*. Those are different problems, and the second one is the unclaimed territory.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Third, the credibility gap and the cheapest way to close it

The talk asserts a failure mode in graph runtimes. Right now you'd be asserting it from architecture. What makes it undeniable is a side-by-side:

- **A:** the same workflow as a naive LangGraph graph — nodes shell out, edges are plain control flow. Approve, push a commit, resume. It applies the stale approval, because a checkpoint is a checkpoint.
- **B:** the same graph with ThreadLoop owning the edges. Identical sequence. It fails closed with a named guard decision in the audit ledger.

That's ~100 lines of demo harness *outside both repos* — it doesn't violate the anti-bloat boundary, and it puts a real graph runtime on stage so you're not straw-manning one. It's also the single highest-value video you could record.

## Fourth, the voice canon

Found it: `~/.codex/skills/voice-canon/` — 16 files, ~3,200 lines. It's already ~95% harness-agnostic: standard `name`/`description` frontmatter, plain Markdown references, and a `routing.md` that selects the minimal canon subset per task. The only Codex-specific artifact is `agents/openai.yaml`. Porting it to `~/.claude/skills/voice-canon/` is minutes, not a project — I'd rather do that as a side task than treat it as a milestone.

One thing I'd flag: the canon files are Drive snapshots with `Refresh checked: 2026-06-18` headers. Six weeks stale. Worth deciding whether the agnostic version pulls fresh or pins the snapshot.

content.content:
| `reviewing -> ready_for_human`         | Current verified signed-review evidence without blockers                                            |
| `ready_for_human -> repairing`         | A later current-HEAD signed-review receipt introduces a blocker                                     |
| `ready_for_human -> completed`         | Current receipt observes a same-HEAD human `User` approval and the PR merged                        |
| `verifying -> blocked`                 | Explicit block evidence after post-PR repair exhaustion (or the existing general blocking contract) |

Always forbidden are `reviewing -> implementing`, post-PR `verifying -> implementing`, `pre_pr_reviewing -> repairing`,
and a fourth post-PR repair entry.

## Pre-PR review evidence

Pre-PR review is provider-neutral transition input, not a signed-review receipt:

```json
{
  "pre_pr_review": {
    "outcome": "changes_required",
    "head_sha": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567",
    "evidence_ref": "review-ledger:2026-07-30",
    "evidence_sha256": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa",
    "findings": [
      {
        "id": "capture-auth-no-mutation",
        "summary": "Capture auth rejection coverage does not prove no mutation.",
        "path": "tests/payments.test.ts"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The HEAD must equal the live repository HEAD. `changes_required` needs at least one uniquely identified normalized
finding; `clean` needs an empty findings array. Recording the evidence is one explicit transition action. Repository
work happens only in a later serialized wake. `session next` returns
`PRE_PR_REVIEW_OUTCOME_REQUIRED -> RECORD_PRE_PR_REVIEW_OUTCOME` when operator/controller input is required.

The initial implementation basis is the proof-plan baseline. A failed local receipt replaces it with that receipt's
HEAD, and review findings replace it with their reviewed HEAD. `implementing -> verifying` requires a clean commit that
descends from and differs from this exact basis. Every implementation or repair commit makes earlier local, signed-CI,
pre-PR review, and signed-review evidence stale unless the evidence contract binds the new HEAD.

`threadloop session gate run <gate-id> --session <id>` executes only the argv, repository-relative working directory,
and timeout stored in the plan. It uses no shell, records stdout/stderr digests and a manifest, appends the receipt
after the child closes, and never advances lifecycle state. A new commit makes old receipts stale without mutating them.

`threadloop session gate import <package-path> --session <id>` verifies the immutable v2/v3 GitHub/Sigstore CI policy,
appends one accepted signed-CI projection, and likewise never advances lifecycle state. See
[Signed gate receipt v1](attestations/receipt-v1.md).

`threadloop session review import <package-path> --session <id>` verifies the independent v3 review policy and appends
one current-HEAD review projection without advancing lifecycle state. The latest valid receipt controls blocker,
approval, and merge projections. See [Signed review receipt v1](attestations/review-v1.md).

Re-entering verification after post-PR gate or signed-review repair requires a clean committed change after the exact
evidence basis that opened that repair. Pre-PR iterations never enter `repairing`, even when a migrated session already
has three historical repair entries. Entering the third repair exhausts new-entry authority but does not prevent that
repair from being committed, verified, and returned to review. An attempted fourth repair instead requires an explicit
evidence-bearing transition to `blocked`.

## Audit coverage

New sessions begin with `session_started`. Sessions created before schema v6 receive exactly one `audit_activated`
genesis event with `coverage: schema_v6_forward`; ThreadLoop does not invent earlier decisions. Audit corruption blocks
controller writes and export but leaves semantic note reads available for diagnosis. `session next` is a read-only
projection and creates no audit event.

evidence basis that opened that repair. Pre-PR iterations never enter `repairing`, even when a migrated session already
has three historical repair entries. Entering the third repair exhausts new-entry authority but does not prevent that
repair from being committed, verified, and returned to review. An attempted fourth repair instead requires an explicit
evidence-bearing transition to `blocked`.

## Audit coverage

New sessions begin with `session_started`. Sessions created before schema v6 receive exactly one `audit_activated`
genesis event with `coverage: schema_v6_forward`; ThreadLoop does not invent earlier decisions. Audit corruption blocks
controller writes and export but leaves semantic note reads available for diagnosis. `session next` is a read-only
projection and creates no audit event.

content.content:
# Governed Coding-Agent Harness

This package is the runnable coding-agent example for the five gates in this
repository. The harness owns the loop. OpenAI and Anthropic adapters translate
provider messages, but they cannot execute tools, approve requests, advance the
lifecycle, verify work, or declare success.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["Provider adapter"] --> H["Governed harness"]
  H --> G["Five deterministic gates"]
  G --> A["Exact-subject approval"]
  G --> C["Local stdio MCP client"]
  C --> S["Offline non-root task container"]
  S --> V["Clean verifier container"]
  V --> E["Content-addressed receipt"]
  E --> J["Out-of-band adjudicator"]
```

The implementation uses the frozen BoundaryBench evaluator for every gate
decision and exposes only five repository tools:

- `repo.list`
- `repo.read`
- `repo.apply_patch`
- `repo.run`
- `repo.diff`

`repo.run` takes an executable, argument array, and working directory. It never
accepts shell text. Node and npm commands execute in a disposable copy of the
current workspace, so test-side writes cannot mutate the governed source;
read-only `git status` and `git diff` inspect the real workspace. The MCP process
and task run in a container with networking disabled, a read-only root
filesystem, no Linux capabilities, a non-root user, and fixed CPU, memory, and
PID limits. Provider keys stay in the host process.
Verifier-only tests are mounted into separate clean containers and are never
available to the task or MCP process.

## What the harness enforces

The lifecycle is:

```text
created → preparing → planning → awaiting_approval → executing → verifying → terminal
```

A model response cannot advance it directly. The first source mutation
receives all four pre-execution decisions, completion receives an
exact-workspace verification decision, and later protected actions are
re-evaluated. Approvals bind the run, task, subject digest, scope, actor, policy
rule, and event position. Changed capability digests invalidate prior trust.
Missing usage fails closed. Cleanup failure changes the terminal result to
`infrastructure_failed`.

Each receipt contains lifecycle events, challenge decisions, approvals,
redacted provider-visible inputs and outputs, raw provider usage fields,
attributed cost, patch and workspace digests, verifier and adjudicator evidence,
cleanup status, and a digest over the complete receipt. It does not request or
persist hidden reasoning.

## Test without provider calls

From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build
npm run test:harness
npm run typecheck
```

The fake-model end-to-end suite proves the governed condition and each
one-gate record-only condition without API keys. The real stdio MCP transport is
also exercised locally. Docker integration runs when both variables are
present. The task image must contain both Node 20 and Git:

```bash
docker pull node:20-bullseye
export BOUNDARYBENCH_DOCKER_TEST=1
export BOUNDARYBENCH_DOCKER_IMAGE="$(
  docker image inspect node:20-bullseye \
    --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
)"
npm run test:harness
```

## Interactive demonstration

Build first, set one provider key on the host, and use an immutable Node 20
image reference:

```bash
export GOVERN_DOCKER_IMAGE='node@sha256:<resolved-digest>'
npm run govern-agent -- doctor --provider openai

export BOUNDARYBENCH_LIVE=1
npm run govern-agent -- run \
  --task capture-idempotency \
  --provider openai \
  --approval interactive
```

The operator must type `approve <exact digest>` for each approval. Interactive
decisions are recorded as `interactive-operator` and are excluded from the
batch experiment. Evidence is written under the ignored `.boundarybench/`
directory.

No live provider call is made by build, test, type-check, or CI.

## Source and claim boundary

content.content:
# Audit export and OpenTelemetry

ThreadLoop's audit ledger is the lifecycle authority. OpenTelemetry is an optional export consumer: it may ship, retain,
and query verified JSONL records, but telemetry input can never authorize or alter a ThreadLoop transition.

## Export

Verify and create a new export:

```bash
threadloop audit export \
  --session "$SESSION_ID" \
  --output ./threadloop-audit.jsonl \
  --json
```

ThreadLoop verifies the complete local chain before export. It writes canonical records shaped as:

```json
{ "event": { "schema_version": 1, "sequence": 1 }, "event_sha256": "0123456789abcdef..." }
```

The command publishes with an exclusive sibling temporary file and refuses to overwrite an existing target. Retain the
reported audit root outside the local database if you need to detect later tail truncation.

`audit show` and `audit verify` do not apply lifecycle transitions once schema v6 is active. Use `threadloop init` for
the explicit schema-v7 semantic migration; prior audit events and honest forward-only coverage remain unchanged.

## Collector recipe

The OpenTelemetry Collector `filelog` receiver can consume completed exports:

```yaml
receivers:
  filelog/threadloop_audit:
    include:
      - /var/log/threadloop/*.jsonl
    start_at: beginning
    include_file_name: true
    operators:
      - type: json_parser
        parse_from: body

processors:
  resource/threadloop_audit:
    attributes:
      - key: service.name
        value: threadloop-audit
        action: upsert

exporters:
  otlp:
    endpoint: ${env:OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT}

service:
  pipelines:
    logs/threadloop_audit:
      receivers: [filelog/threadloop_audit]
      processors: [resource/threadloop_audit]
      exporters: [otlp]
```

Configure the destination and authentication according to the chosen collector deployment. Rotate exports by creating a
new filename; do not modify or append to a published ThreadLoop export.

## Authority boundary

- SQLite stores the append-only audit events and lifecycle state.
- `threadloop audit verify` establishes local chain integrity and can compare a retained external root.
- `threadloop audit export` is a verified projection.
- The Collector and downstream telemetry store are read-only consumers of that projection.
- A dashboard, alert, missing log, or ingested JSONL record is never evidence for a lifecycle transition.

=== RUNTIME ACCOUNTABILITY PATTERN ===
# Pattern: Runtime Accountability

## Problem The Pattern Solves

Autonomous workflows can be technically running while remaining operationally invisible. Runtime accountability exists so teams can supervise authority, trace activity, and intervene when spend or quota thresholds are crossed.

## Why The Common Shortcut Fails

The shortcut is: "log a few events and add a dashboard later." That misses the real job. Runtime accountability is not passive observability. It is the gate that makes execution state, traceability, quota, and spend governable while the system is still acting.

## Pattern Definition

Runtime accountability should:

1. expose meaningful execution state and current phase
2. tie usage and spend back to a request, session, team, or workflow
3. evaluate quota, balance, or policy thresholds during execution
4. require explicit allow, ask, or stop behavior when thresholds are crossed

The standard is simple: if the system can act autonomously, operators should be able to see what it is doing, where it is running, and what it is costing while it runs.

## Minimal Example

```text
Runtime accountability layer:
- record execution target and current phase
- attach usage to a request or trace ID
- evaluate quota and spend thresholds
- alert, ask, block, or stop explicitly when limits are crossed
```

## Copied/Adapted Code Receipt

> Adapted from a private production codebase; trimmed and renamed for clarity.

```ts
pollRemoteSession(sessionId, update => {
  setRunState({
    phase: update.phase,
    executionTarget: update.executionTarget,
    rejectCount: update.rejectCount,
  })
})
```

This receipt matters because remote authority should not change silently. Operators need inspectable state while a workflow is still live.

export function checkOverageGate(context) {
  if (!context.extraUsageEnabled) return { outcome: 'block' }
  if (context.lowBalance) return { outcome: 'ask', reason: 'low_balance' }
  return { outcome: 'continue' }
}

Autonomous workflows can be technically running while remaining operationally invisible. Runtime accountability exists so teams can supervise authority, trace activity, and intervene when spend or quota thresholds are crossed.

## Why The Common Shortcut Fails

The shortcut is: "log a few events and add a dashboard later." That misses the real job. Runtime accountability is not passive observability. It is the gate that makes execution state, traceability, quota, and spend governable while the system is still acting.

## Pattern Definition

Runtime accountability should:

1. expose meaningful execution state and current phase
2. tie usage and spend back to a request, session, team, or workflow
3. evaluate quota, balance, or policy thresholds during execution
4. require explicit allow, ask, or stop behavior when thresholds are crossed

The standard is simple: if the system can act autonomously, operators should be able to see what it is doing, where it is running, and what it is costing while it runs.

## Minimal Example

```text
Runtime accountability layer:
- record execution target and current phase
- attach usage to a request or trace ID
- evaluate quota and spend thresholds
- alert, ask, block, or stop explicitly when limits are crossed
```

# Seven Controls: Coverage, Proof Gap, and Claim Options

**Date:** 2026-07-30
**Question:** What is left to build in ThreadLoop and Governed Agent Autonomy Patterns before there is
technical proof strong enough to carry a conference talk, a technical breakdown, and video content?
**Method:** Verified against local checkouts and live GitHub state on 2026-07-30. Every capability claim
below cites a file, doc section, or command that exists today.

---

## 1. Verified current state

| | Value on 2026-07-30 | Note |
|---|---|---|
| ThreadLoop `main` | `6a59de9` | +4 PRs past the 2026-07-29 assessment (#70, #72, #74, #76) |
| ThreadLoop runner skill | **landed on `main`** | `.agents/skills/threadloop-runner/SKILL.md` + `references/wake-record.md`, `references/handoff.md` |
| ThreadLoop protocol / schema | **contract v4 / SQLite v7** | prior assessment said v3 / v6; a `pre_pr_reviewing` state was added |
| ThreadLoop open work | **1 issue (#46, esbuild bump)** | no open PRs, clean working tree |
| ThreadLoop source size | 13,531 LOC TypeScript | 52 source files |
| Governed `main` | `6316a77` | unchanged since PR #5 merged |
| Governed harness size | 3,934 LOC (`examples/governed-coding-agent/src`) | `harness.ts` is 1,225 LOC |
| Governed open work | 1 issue (#1, deferred explorer) | attempt-admission plan **not implemented** |
| SignalPay `main` | `a6e832c` | **no `.threadloop/`, no runner skill, no session — pilot never ran** |
| Live runs, either project | **zero** | Governed README states this explicitly |

**The single most important fact:** ThreadLoop's backlog is empty and neither project has ever produced a
live run. The architecture questions are answered. None of the empirical ones are.

---

## 2. The seven controls, scored against what exists

Source of the seven: the "Graph Is Not the Factory" failure→control→proof structure developed
2026-07-29. Scoring is `built` / `partial` / `gap` / `structurally excluded`.

### Control 1 — Retries must not duplicate external actions

*Solution shape: durable intent records, stable idempotency keys, tool receipts, deduplication, compensation.*

- **ThreadLoop: built.** `session transition` requires the caller's expected state version **and** an
  idempotency key. State mutation, transition history, idempotency outcome, audit guard decision, active
  projection, and session completion are one SQLite transaction (`docs/lifecycle.md:51`). Exact replays add
  no duplicate events; a changed request under the same key returns `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`; a rejected guard
  retains unchanged lifecycle plus one idempotent `guard_decision`. The gate runner appends its receipt only
  after the child process closes.
- **Governed: gap.** The experiment runner treats any cell without a terminal receipt as pending. A crash
  after provider spend but before `AtomicEvidenceSink.write` makes that cell eligible for silent replay —
  duplicate spend, and a second stochastic sample replacing the declared single sample. The write-once
  attempt-admission plan exists and is unimplemented.
- **Verdict:** covered on the lifecycle side, open on the execution side. **One PR closes it.**

### Control 2 — Parallel agents must not create conflicting state and patches

*Solution shape: isolated workspaces, typed state reducers, artifact ownership, deterministic joins, conflict escalation.*

- **ThreadLoop: structurally excluded.** It has optimistic concurrency (`expected_state_version` →
  `STATE_VERSION_CONFLICT`), which serializes *competing writers to one session*. It does not merge parallel
  work. The runner skill requires one session bound to one dedicated worktree and assigns serialization to
  the scheduler. ThreadLoop *avoids* parallelism rather than governing it.
- **Governed: isolation only.** Each attempt runs in a disposable workspace copy inside a container. One
  attempt at a time. No joins, no reducers, no conflict escalation.
- **Verdict:** **not covered, and deliberately so.** Both projects' anti-bloat boundaries forbid adding it.

### Control 3 — Approvals must not go stale

*Solution shape: bind approval to artifact hash, repository revision, policy version, proposed action, expiry.*

- **ThreadLoop: built, and this is the strongest surface in either project.**
  `ready_for_human -> completed` requires a current receipt observing a same-HEAD human `User` approval
  **and** an observed PR merge. `ready_for_human -> repairing` fires when a later current-HEAD signed-review
  receipt introduces a blocker — approval is revocable by new evidence. `docs/lifecycle.md` states that every
  implementation or repair commit makes earlier local, signed-CI, pre-PR review, and signed-review evidence
  stale unless the evidence contract binds the new HEAD.
- **Governed: built.** Approvals bind the run, task, subject digest, scope, actor, policy rule, and event
  position. Changed capability digests invalidate prior trust. The operator must type `approve <exact digest>`.
- **Verdict:** **fully covered on both sides.** This is the demo.

### Control 4 — Replay must be reproducible across version change

*Solution shape: a run manifest pinning graph, state schema, prompt, model, tool contract, policy, evaluator versions.*

- **ThreadLoop: built for its own topology.** Contract v4 and SQLite v7 with a transactional migration.
  Reading schema v6 returns `migration_required` **without mutation**. Migrated sessions receive exactly one
  `audit_activated` genesis event with `coverage: schema_v6_forward` — it refuses to invent earlier decisions.
  Immutable proof plans. This is control 4 applied to live sessions crossing a schema change.
- **Governed: built for its own runs.** Frozen manifest with digest, experiment schemas at `v0.2.0`, receipt
  schema `boundarybench.receipt.v0.1.0`, frozen evaluator, provider contract fixtures, pinned Docker image
  digest, documented UTC pricing validity boundary.
- **Verdict:** covered *within* each project. **No joint manifest spans both**, and Governed's manifest
  freeze has not been executed.

### Control 5 — An allowed edge must not become an authorization bypass

*Solution shape: per-node workload identity, least-privilege capabilities, trusted state labels, sandboxing, action-scoped authorization.*

- **Governed: built, thoroughly.** Exactly five repository tools (`repo.list`, `repo.read`,
  `repo.apply_patch`, `repo.run`, `repo.diff`). `repo.run` takes an executable, argv array, and working
  directory — never shell text. Container has networking disabled, read-only root filesystem, no Linux
  capabilities, non-root user, fixed CPU/memory/PID limits. Verifier-only tests mount into separate clean
  containers and are never visible to the task or MCP process. Provider keys stay in the host process.
  BoundaryBench has a dedicated `config-path-jail` task.
- **ThreadLoop: partial by design.** Signed CI and signed review receipts carry Sigstore/GitHub OIDC
  identity binding — identity-bound *evidence* authorization. ThreadLoop holds no model, tool, or sandbox
  policy, per its explicit boundary.
- **Verdict:** covered, and it is the cleanest division-of-labor story in the set — Governed owns execution
  authorization, ThreadLoop owns evidence-identity authorization.

### Control 6 — Traces show activity, not correctness

*Solution shape: connect execution traces to node, transition, trajectory, outcome, and policy evaluations.*

- **ThreadLoop: built, and stated as an architectural boundary.** `docs/observability.md` makes the audit
  ledger the lifecycle authority and OpenTelemetry a read-only export consumer, closing with: *"A dashboard,
  alert, missing log, or ingested JSONL record is never evidence for a lifecycle transition."* Rejected
  transitions persist a `guard_decision`, so refusals are as auditable as successes. `audit export` verifies
  the complete chain, refuses to overwrite, and reports a root for external tail-truncation detection.
- **Governed: built.** Independent verifier runs in a clean container against the exact workspace digest.
  Out-of-band adjudicator. BoundaryBench runs 35/35 conformance with 5/5 unsafe mutants caught — evidence
  that the evaluator discriminates, not merely that it runs.
- **Verdict:** **fully covered on both sides.**

### Control 7 — Fan-out destroys the economics

*Solution shape: branch-level token, tool, retry, concurrency, and latency budgets with admission control and early termination.*

- **Governed: built at single-attempt granularity.** `harness.ts` enforces warn / approval / hard-stop
  cost thresholds in micros, `maxToolCalls`, `maxModelTurns`, `maxInputTokens`, `maxOutputTokens`,
  `trialTimeoutMs`, `requestTimeoutMs`. Missing usage fails closed. Exhaustion produces a `budget_stopped`
  terminal state with a stated recovery path.
- **ThreadLoop: partial.** A three-entry post-PR repair budget is a retry budget at lifecycle granularity.
  Exhausting it requires an explicit evidence-bearing transition to `blocked`. No token or cost concept, by
  design.
- **Verdict:** the *per-attempt* half is covered well. The *fan-out* half is not covered, for the same
  reason as control 2 — there is no fan-out.

### Coverage summary

| Control | ThreadLoop | Governed | Together | Work left |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Duplicate external actions | built | **gap** | partial | 1 PR (attempt admission) |
| 2. Parallel conflicting state | excluded | isolation only | **not covered** | structurally out of scope |
| 3. Stale approvals | **built** | **built** | **strong** | none — run it |
| 4. Reproducible replay | built | built | strong within, no joint manifest | optional joint manifest |
| 5. Edge ≠ authorization | partial by design | **built** | **strong** | none — run it |
| 6. Traces ≠ correctness | **built** | **built** | **strong** | none — run it |
| 7. Fan-out economics | partial | built per-attempt | partial | fan-out half out of scope |

**Four of seven are strongly covered by the pair. One needs a single PR. Two are structurally excluded.**

---

## 3. The finding that changes the claim

Controls 2 and the fan-out half of 7 are the two controls that **only matter when a graph has parallel
branches**. Both projects deliberately assume serial execution — one session bound to one worktree, one
attempt at a time. Their anti-bloat boundaries explicitly forbid adding schedulers, queues, or DAG engines.

So a talk that promises to address all seven cannot be delivered honestly from these two systems. That is
not a shortfall. It is the most interesting result in this analysis, and it should become part of the claim
rather than a gap to hide:

> The two controls these systems do not implement are the two that only exist because the graph fanned out.
> Everything that actually broke in a coding workflow broke serially.

---

## 4. The honesty problem nobody has flagged yet

The 2026-07-29 seam memo deliberately deferred the receipt importer: the two projects have **incompatible
receipt formats and no code dependency**. That was the right engineering call.

It creates a narrative liability. Any claim that the two tools "work in tandem" is currently describing an
unbuilt integration. Two honest options:

1. **Operator-connected pipeline.** Present them as two authorities in one supervised pipeline, connected by
   an operator who carries `change.patch` and `execution-receipt.json` between them. This is exactly what the
   SignalPay pilot will actually show. Zero build cost. Fully honest.
2. **Thin demo-only receipt bridge.** A small adapter, living outside both repos, that wraps a Governed
   execution receipt with ThreadLoop's session/gate/repo/branch/HEAD identities. Makes the handoff visible on
   stage. Must be presented as a research bridge, not a product seam.

Option 1 is sufficient for the first talk. Option 2 is the better second artifact.

---

## 5. Minimum path to technical proof

Ordered by leverage per unit of work. Nothing here requires new product surface area.

### A. Run the SignalPay consumer-repository pilot — **zero code**

The plan is written and the runner skill is on `main`. This is the one artifact that is simultaneously the
CFP's proof, the technical case study, the video, and the article. It exercises controls 1, 3, 4, and 6 live.

Acceptance already specified: fresh worktree, explicit session, capture-state safety feature, red tests
first, one clean implementation commit, ThreadLoop-run `make verify`, signed CI and review import, at least
one wake resumed in a **fresh Codex context**, stop at `ready_for_human`, verified audit export.

### B. Governed attempt admission — **one PR**

Write-once flushed marker before `createModel`/`runTrial`; derived states `never_started` / `finalized` /
`uncertain` / `invalid`; resume only `never_started`; stop the whole run set on uncertain or invalid. Closes
control 1's open half.

### C. Freeze and run the 60-cell BoundaryBench pilot — **provider spend, post-B**

The only source of quantitative numbers in the entire story. Five tasks × two providers × six conditions.
Produces cost, refusal, and verification-discrimination data that a stage audience can interrogate.

### D. The naive-vs-guarded A/B harness — **~150 lines, outside both repos**

The one artifact nobody planned, and the one that turns an assertion into a demonstration:

- **Run A:** the same workflow as a plain graph (LangGraph or ADK), nodes shelling out, edges as control
  flow. Approve. Push a commit. Resume from checkpoint. It applies the stale approval, because a checkpoint
  is a checkpoint.
- **Run B:** identical sequence, ThreadLoop owning the edges. It fails closed with a named `guard_decision`
  in the audit ledger.

This puts a real graph runtime on stage, so the argument is not a straw man, and it does not add a graph DSL
to either product. It is the highest-value 150 lines available.

### What is explicitly NOT on this path

Rust rewrite, BoundaryBench explorer, graph DSL, scheduler, queue, lease service, wake-lease infrastructure,
parallel merge governor, receipt importer as product surface, cloud persistence, dashboard.

---

## 6. Claim options

Presented for selection. Each is scored on what it needs and what it risks.

### Angle A — Staleness over parallelism

> Most coding-agent failures are not parallelism failures. They are staleness failures. The dangerous edge
> is not the fan-out join; it is the resume after the world moved.

- Covers controls 1, 3, 4, 6 honestly. Declares 2 and 7-fanout out of scope with a stated reason.
- Needs: A + B + D.
- Risk: reviewers expecting "graph engineering" may read it as narrower than the label promised.
- Strength: lowest build cost, fully provable, and the honesty is itself credible on stage.

### Angle B — Fan-out is a research pattern, not a coding pattern

> Graph engineering imported fan-out from research agents, where parallel search works, into coding agents,
> where it mostly manufactures merge conflicts and cost. These two systems are the existence proof that
> serial-with-guards beats parallel-without.

- Turns the two uncovered controls into *evidence for the thesis* rather than gaps.
- Supported externally: Anthropic reports ~15× chat token usage in its multi-agent research workload and
  notes coding has fewer genuinely parallelizable tasks.
- Needs: A + B + C (the cost numbers carry this one) + D.
- Risk: it is a contrarian claim against the current direction of LangChain, Google ADK, and AutoGen. It
  needs the quantitative pilot or it reads as rationalization.
- Strength: most differentiated. Nobody else is arguing this.

### Angle C — Edges are admission decisions over expiring evidence

> A graph runtime models an edge as control flow and a checkpoint as durable truth. Neither has a concept of
> stale. Software delivery is made almost entirely of evidence that expires the moment someone pushes.

- Grounded verbatim in `docs/lifecycle.md:36`: *"Structural permission is not evidence that a transition
  should occur."*
- Needs: A + D. B and C optional.
- Risk: it is a mechanism claim, so the A/B demo is mandatory — without it, this is a definition.
- Strength: the sharpest single sentence available, and it makes `docs/lifecycle.md` the citation.

### Angle D — Execution authority is not lifecycle authority

> A successful agent run must not be able to complete the task it ran for. Those are two different
> authorities, and collapsing them is how "the agent said it passed" becomes "the work shipped."

- Fully built on both sides today. Provable with the pilot alone.
- Needs: A. D strengthens it. B and C not required.
- Risk: least tied to the graph-engineering label; it is an architecture claim about authority separation.
- Strength: most original, least crowded, cheapest to prove, and it is the invariant the 2026-07-29 memo
  already identified as critical.

### Not viable

**Claim all seven.** Would require building a parallel-branch merge governor, violating both anti-bloat
boundaries, and it is not finishable before the October 11 deadline.

---

## 7. Calendar

- **2026-07-30** — today
- **2026-09-15** — CFP early-review target (6.5 weeks)
- **2026-10-11** — CFP final deadline (10.5 weeks)
- Up to three proposals accepted; historical acceptance 5–15%; primary format 15–20 minute stage talks

Six and a half weeks is enough for A + B + D comfortably, and for C if the pilot starts within two weeks.

---

## 8. Evidence boundary for this document

Verified from local checkouts at ThreadLoop `6a59de9`, Governed `6316a77`, SignalPay `a6e832c`, and live
GitHub issue/PR state on 2026-07-30. Capability claims cite existing files, documented CLI behavior, or
README statements. No live run, pilot result, empirical number, or integration between the two projects
exists as of this date. External figures attributed to Anthropic and CFP details were established in prior
research and are not re-verified here — re-check before any public use.

*Solution shape: durable intent records, stable idempotency keys, tool receipts, deduplication, compensation.*

- **ThreadLoop: built.** `session transition` requires the caller's expected state version **and** an
  idempotency key. State mutation, transition history, idempotency outcome, audit guard decision, active
  projection, and session completion are one SQLite transaction (`docs/lifecycle.md:51`). Exact replays add
  no duplicate events; a changed request under the same key returns `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`; a rejected guard
  retains unchanged lifecycle plus one idempotent `guard_decision`. The gate runner appends its receipt only
  after the child process closes.
- **Governed: gap.** The experiment runner treats any cell without a terminal receipt as pending. A crash
  after provider spend but before `AtomicEvidenceSink.write` makes that cell eligible for silent replay —
  duplicate spend, and a second stochastic sample replacing the declared single sample. The write-once
  attempt-admission plan exists and is unimplemented.
- **Verdict:** covered on the lifecycle side, open on the execution side. **One PR closes it.**

### Control 2 — Parallel agents must not create conflicting state and patches

*Solution shape: isolated workspaces, typed state reducers, artifact ownership, deterministic joins, conflict escalation.*

- **ThreadLoop: structurally excluded.** It has optimistic concurrency (`expected_state_version` →
  `STATE_VERSION_CONFLICT`), which serializes *competing writers to one session*. It does not merge parallel
  work. The runner skill requires one session bound to one dedicated worktree and assigns serialization to
  the scheduler. ThreadLoop *avoids* parallelism rather than governing it.
- **Governed: isolation only.** Each attempt runs in a disposable workspace copy inside a container. One
  attempt at a time. No joins, no reducers, no conflict escalation.
- **Verdict:** **not covered, and deliberately so.** Both projects' anti-bloat boundaries forbid adding it.

### Control 3 — Approvals must not go stale

*Solution shape: bind approval to artifact hash, repository revision, policy version, proposed action, expiry.*

- **ThreadLoop: built, and this is the strongest surface in either project.**
  `ready_for_human -> completed` requires a current receipt observing a same-HEAD human `User` approval
  **and** an observed PR merge. `ready_for_human -> repairing` fires when a later current-HEAD signed-review
  receipt introduces a blocker — approval is revocable by new evidence. `docs/lifecycle.md` states that every
  implementation or repair commit makes earlier local, signed-CI, pre-PR review, and signed-review evidence
  stale unless the evidence contract binds the new HEAD.
- **Governed: built.** Approvals bind the run, task, subject digest, scope, actor, policy rule, and event
  position. Changed capability digests invalidate prior trust. The operator must type `approve <exact digest>`.
- **Verdict:** **fully covered on both sides.** This is the demo.

### Control 4 — Replay must be reproducible across version change

*Solution shape: a run manifest pinning graph, state schema, prompt, model, tool contract, policy, evaluator versions.*

- **ThreadLoop: built for its own topology.** Contract v4 and SQLite v7 with a transactional migration.
  Reading schema v6 returns `migration_required` **without mutation**. Migrated sessions receive exactly one
  `audit_activated` genesis event with `coverage: schema_v6_forward` — it refuses to invent earlier decisions.
  Immutable proof plans. This is control 4 applied to live sessions crossing a schema change.
- **Governed: built for its own runs.** Frozen manifest with digest, experiment schemas at `v0.2.0`, receipt
  schema `boundarybench.receipt.v0.1.0`, frozen evaluator, provider contract fixtures, pinned Docker image
  digest, documented UTC pricing validity boundary.
- **Verdict:** covered *within* each project. **No joint manifest spans both**, and Governed's manifest
  freeze has not been executed.

### Control 5 — An allowed edge must not become an authorization bypass

*Solution shape: per-node workload identity, least-privilege capabilities, trusted state labels, sandboxing, action-scoped authorization.*

- **Governed: built, thoroughly.** Exactly five repository tools (`repo.list`, `repo.read`,
  `repo.apply_patch`, `repo.run`, `repo.diff`). `repo.run` takes an executable, argv array, and working
  directory — never shell text. Container has networking disabled, read-only root filesystem, no Linux
  capabilities, non-root user, fixed CPU/memory/PID limits. Verifier-only tests mount into separate clean
  containers and are never visible to the task or MCP process. Provider keys stay in the host process.
  BoundaryBench has a dedicated `config-path-jail` task.
- **ThreadLoop: partial by design.** Signed CI and signed review receipts carry Sigstore/GitHub OIDC
  identity binding — identity-bound *evidence* authorization. ThreadLoop holds no model, tool, or sandbox
  policy, per its explicit boundary.
- **Verdict:** covered, and it is the cleanest division-of-labor story in the set — Governed owns execution
  authorization, ThreadLoop owns evidence-identity authorization.

### Control 6 — Traces show activity, not correctness

*Solution shape: connect execution traces to node, transition, trajectory, outcome, and policy evaluations.*

- **ThreadLoop: built, and stated as an architectural boundary.** `docs/observability.md` makes the audit
  ledger the lifecycle authority and OpenTelemetry a read-only export consumer, closing with: *"A dashboard,
  alert, missing log, or ingested JSONL record is never evidence for a lifecycle transition."* Rejected
  transitions persist a `guard_decision`, so refusals are as auditable as successes. `audit export` verifies
  the complete chain, refuses to overwrite, and reports a root for external tail-truncation detection.
- **Governed: built.** Independent verifier runs in a clean container against the exact workspace digest.
  Out-of-band adjudicator. BoundaryBench runs 35/35 conformance with 5/5 unsafe mutants caught — evidence
  that the evaluator discriminates, not merely that it runs.
- **Verdict:** **fully covered on both sides.**

### Control 7 — Fan-out destroys the economics

*Solution shape: branch-level token, tool, retry, concurrency, and latency budgets with admission control and early termination.*

- **Governed: built at single-attempt granularity.** `harness.ts` enforces warn / approval / hard-stop
  cost thresholds in micros, `maxToolCalls`, `maxModelTurns`, `maxInputTokens`, `maxOutputTokens`,
  `trialTimeoutMs`, `requestTimeoutMs`. Missing usage fails closed. Exhaustion produces a `budget_stopped`
  terminal state with a stated recovery path.
- **ThreadLoop: partial.** A three-entry post-PR repair budget is a retry budget at lifecycle granularity.
  Exhausting it requires an explicit evidence-bearing transition to `blocked`. No token or cost concept, by
  design.
- **Verdict:** the *per-attempt* half is covered well. The *fan-out* half is not covered, for the same
  reason as control 2 — there is no fan-out.

### Coverage summary

| Control | ThreadLoop | Governed | Together | Work left |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Duplicate external actions | built | **gap** | partial | 1 PR (attempt admission) |
| 2. Parallel conflicting state | excluded | isolation only | **not covered** | structurally out of scope |
| 3. Stale approvals | **built** | **built** | **strong** | none — run it |
| 4. Reproducible replay | built | built | strong within, no joint manifest | optional joint manifest |
| 5. Edge ≠ authorization | partial by design | **built** | **strong** | none — run it |
| 6. Traces ≠ correctness | **built** | **built** | **strong** | none — run it |
| 7. Fan-out economics | partial | built per-attempt | partial | fan-out half out of scope |

**Four of seven are strongly covered by the pair. One needs a single PR. Two are structurally excluded.**

---

## 3. The finding that changes the claim

Controls 2 and the fan-out half of 7 are the two controls that **only matter when a graph has parallel
branches**. Both projects deliberately assume serial execution — one session bound to one worktree, one
attempt at a time. Their anti-bloat boundaries explicitly forbid adding schedulers, queues, or DAG engines.

So a talk that promises to address all seven cannot be delivered honestly from these two systems. That is
not a shortfall. It is the most interesting result in this analysis, and it should become part of the claim
rather than a gap to hide:

> The two controls these systems do not implement are the two that only exist because the graph fanned out.
> Everything that actually broke in a coding workflow broke serially.

---

## 4. The honesty problem nobody has flagged yet

The 2026-07-29 seam memo deliberately deferred the receipt importer: the two projects have **incompatible
receipt formats and no code dependency**. That was the right engineering call.

It creates a narrative liability. Any claim that the two tools "work in tandem" is currently describing an
unbuilt integration. Two honest options:

1. **Operator-connected pipeline.** Present them as two authorities in one supervised pipeline, connected by
   an operator who carries `change.patch` and `execution-receipt.json` between them. This is exactly what the
   SignalPay pilot will actually show. Zero build cost. Fully honest.
2. **Thin demo-only receipt bridge.** A small adapter, living outside both repos, that wraps a Governed
   execution receipt with ThreadLoop's session/gate/repo/branch/HEAD identities. Makes the handoff visible on
   stage. Must be presented as a research bridge, not a product seam.

Option 1 is sufficient for the first talk. Option 2 is the better second artifact.

---

## 5. Minimum path to technical proof

Ordered by leverage per unit of work. Nothing here requires new product surface area.

### A. Run the SignalPay consumer-repository pilot — **zero code**

The plan is written and the runner skill is on `main`. This is the one artifact that is simultaneously the
CFP's proof, the technical case study, the video, and the article. It exercises controls 1, 3, 4, and 6 live.

Acceptance already specified: fresh worktree, explicit session, capture-state safety feature, red tests
first, one clean implementation commit, ThreadLoop-run `make verify`, signed CI and review import, at least
one wake resumed in a **fresh Codex context**, stop at `ready_for_human`, verified audit export.

### B. Governed attempt admission — **one PR**

Write-once flushed marker before `createModel`/`runTrial`; derived states `never_started` / `finalized` /
`uncertain` / `invalid`; resume only `never_started`; stop the whole run set on uncertain or invalid. Closes
control 1's open half.

### C. Freeze and run the 60-cell BoundaryBench pilot — **provider spend, post-B**

The only source of quantitative numbers in the entire story. Five tasks × two providers × six conditions.
Produces cost, refusal, and verification-discrimination data that a stage audience can interrogate.

### D. The naive-vs-guarded A/B harness — **~150 lines, outside both repos**

The one artifact nobody planned, and the one that turns an assertion into a demonstration:

- **Run A:** the same workflow as a plain graph (LangGraph or ADK), nodes shelling out, edges as control
  flow. Approve. Push a commit. Resume from checkpoint. It applies the stale approval, because a checkpoint
  is a checkpoint.
- **Run B:** identical sequence, ThreadLoop owning the edges. It fails closed with a named `guard_decision`
  in the audit ledger.

This puts a real graph runtime on stage, so the argument is not a straw man, and it does not add a graph DSL
to either product. It is the highest-value 150 lines available.

### What is explicitly NOT on this path

Rust rewrite, BoundaryBench explorer, graph DSL, scheduler, queue, lease service, wake-lease infrastructure,
parallel merge governor, receipt importer as product surface, cloud persistence, dashboard.

---

## 6. Claim options

Presented for selection. Each is scored on what it needs and what it risks.

### Angle A — Staleness over parallelism

> Most coding-agent failures are not parallelism failures. They are staleness failures. The dangerous edge
> is not the fan-out join; it is the resume after the world moved.

- Covers controls 1, 3, 4, 6 honestly. Declares 2 and 7-fanout out of scope with a stated reason.
- Needs: A + B + D.
- Risk: reviewers expecting "graph engineering" may read it as narrower than the label promised.
- Strength: lowest build cost, fully provable, and the honesty is itself credible on stage.

### Angle B — Fan-out is a research pattern, not a coding pattern

> Graph engineering imported fan-out from research agents, where parallel search works, into coding agents,
> where it mostly manufactures merge conflicts and cost. These two systems are the existence proof that
> serial-with-guards beats parallel-without.

- Turns the two uncovered controls into *evidence for the thesis* rather than gaps.
- Supported externally: Anthropic reports ~15× chat token usage in its multi-agent research workload and
  notes coding has fewer genuinely parallelizable tasks.
- Needs: A + B + C (the cost numbers carry this one) + D.
- Risk: it is a contrarian claim against the current direction of LangChain, Google ADK, and AutoGen. It
  needs the quantitative pilot or it reads as rationalization.
- Strength: most differentiated. Nobody else is arguing this.

### Angle C — Edges are admission decisions over expiring evidence

> A graph runtime models an edge as control flow and a checkpoint as durable truth. Neither has a concept of
> stale. Software delivery is made almost entirely of evidence that expires the moment someone pushes.

- Grounded verbatim in `docs/lifecycle.md:36`: *"Structural permission is not evidence that a transition
  should occur."*
- Needs: A + D. B and C optional.
- Risk: it is a mechanism claim, so the A/B demo is mandatory — without it, this is a definition.
- Strength: the sharpest single sentence available, and it makes `docs/lifecycle.md` the citation.

### Angle D — Execution authority is not lifecycle authority

> A successful agent run must not be able to complete the task it ran for. Those are two different
> authorities, and collapsing them is how "the agent said it passed" becomes "the work shipped."

- Fully built on both sides today. Provable with the pilot alone.
- Needs: A. D strengthens it. B and C not required.
- Risk: least tied to the graph-engineering label; it is an architecture claim about authority separation.
- Strength: most original, least crowded, cheapest to prove, and it is the invariant the 2026-07-29 memo
  already identified as critical.

### Not viable

**Claim all seven.** Would require building a parallel-branch merge governor, violating both anti-bloat
boundaries, and it is not finishable before the October 11 deadline.

---

## 7. Calendar

- **2026-07-30** — today
- **2026-09-15** — CFP early-review target (6.5 weeks)
- **2026-10-11** — CFP final deadline (10.5 weeks)
- Up to three proposals accepted; historical acceptance 5–15%; primary format 15–20 minute stage talks

Six and a half weeks is enough for A + B + D comfortably, and for C if the pilot starts within two weeks.

---

## 8. Evidence boundary for this document

Verified from local checkouts at ThreadLoop `6a59de9`, Governed `6316a77`, SignalPay `a6e832c`, and live
GitHub issue/PR state on 2026-07-30. Capability claims cite existing files, documented CLI behavior, or
README statements. No live run, pilot result, empirical number, or integration between the two projects
exists as of this date. External figures attributed to Anthropic and CFP details were established in prior
research and are not re-verified here — re-check before any public use.

## The scorecard

I scored all seven controls against code that exists today, not against the summaries.

| Control | ThreadLoop | Governed | Together |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Retries duplicate external actions | **built** | **gap** | 1 PR closes it |
| 2. Parallel conflicting patches | excluded | isolation only | **not covered** |
| 3. Stale approvals | **built** | **built** | strong |
| 4. Reproducible replay | built | built | strong within each |

| 7. Fan-out economics | partial | built per-attempt | **fan-out half missing** |

Four of seven are genuinely strong across the pair. One needs a single PR — Governed's write-once attempt marker. Two are not covered.

Some of this is stronger than the transcript credited. Control 6 isn't just "ThreadLoop has an audit ledger" — `docs/observability.md` closes with *"A dashboard, alert, missing log, or ingested JSONL record is never evidence for a lifecycle transition."* That's the exact claim of control 6, already written as an architectural boundary. And rejected transitions persist a `guard_decision`, so refusals are as auditable as successes. Most systems can't show you what they refused.

## The finding that should change your claim

Control 2 and the fan-out half of control 7 are **the only two controls that require a graph with parallel branches.** Both your projects assume serial execution — one session bound to one worktree, one attempt at a time — and both anti-bloat boundaries explicitly forbid adding schedulers or DAG engines.

So you cannot honestly promise all seven from these systems. But that's not a shortfall to hide:

> The two controls these systems don't implement are the two that only exist because the graph fanned out. Everything that actually broke in a coding workflow broke serially.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The reason your architecture reads as coherent rather than incomplete: ThreadLoop's guards are predicates over the **external world**, not over internal state. `reviewing -> ready_for_human` doesn't ask "did review happen?" — it asks "is signed review evidence *currently* valid against *this* HEAD?" That inverts the durability problem graph runtimes solve. LangGraph asks *how do I resume without re-running side effects*. Yours asks *how do I refuse to resume when the world moved under the checkpoint*. Serial execution isn't a limitation of that design — it's what makes the question answerable at all. You can't evaluate "current HEAD" against four branches at once.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## The honesty problem nobody flagged

The seam memo deliberately deferred the receipt importer — the two projects have **incompatible receipt formats and zero code dependency.** Right engineering call, but it means any claim that they "work in tandem" currently describes something unbuilt. Two honest routes: present them as two authorities connected by an operator carrying `change.patch` + `execution-receipt.json` (which is what the pilot will actually show, zero cost), or build a thin demo-only receipt bridge outside both repos. The first is enough for talk one.

## What's actually left to build

| | Work | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Run the SignalPay pilot | **zero code** — plan written, runner skill on `main` |
| **B** | Governed attempt admission | one PR, plan already specified |
| **C** | Freeze + run 60-cell BoundaryBench pilot | provider spend, needs B first |
| **D** | Naive-vs-guarded A/B harness | ~150 lines, outside both repos |

**D is the one nobody planned and it's the highest value per line.** Same workflow twice: once as a plain LangGraph graph with nodes shelling out and edges as control flow — approve, push a commit, resume, and it applies the stale approval because a checkpoint is a checkpoint. Then identical sequence with ThreadLoop owning the edges, failing closed with a named `guard_decision`. That puts a real graph runtime on stage so you're not straw-manning one, without adding a graph DSL to either product.

6.5 weeks to Sept 15 covers A + B + D comfortably, and C if the pilot starts within two weeks.

## Four claim angles

I'm not picking for you — here's the honest trade on each.

**A. Staleness over parallelism.** *"The dangerous edge isn't the fan-out join, it's the resume after the world moved."* Covers 1/3/4/6, declares 2 and 7-fanout out of scope with a reason. Needs A+B+D. Cheapest, fully provable. Risk: reads narrower than "graph engineering" promised.

**B. Fan-out is a research pattern, not a coding pattern.** *"Graph engineering imported parallel search from research agents into coding, where it mostly manufactures merge conflicts and cost."* Converts your two uncovered controls into evidence *for* the thesis. Most differentiated — nobody is arguing this. Needs the quantitative pilot (C) or it reads as rationalization. Risk: contrarian against LangChain, ADK, and AutoGen simultaneously.

**C. Edges are admission decisions over expiring evidence.** Grounded verbatim in your own `docs/lifecycle.md:36` — *"Structural permission is not evidence that a transition should occur."* Sharpest single sentence available. Needs A+D; the A/B demo is mandatory or it's just a definition.

**D. Execution authority is not lifecycle authority.** *"A successful agent run must not be able to complete the task it ran for."* Fully built on both sides today, provable with the pilot alone. Most original, least crowded, cheapest. Risk: least tied to the graph label.

Worth noting these aren't mutually exclusive across three CFP submissions — C and D in particular are the same architecture viewed from the edge and from the authority boundary, and B is the one that needs its own evidence base.

Which claim do you want to pressure-test first? I'd rather grill one of these properly than have you pick from a menu — and if you want, I can run the `/grilling` skill against your preferred angle to find where a technical reviewer would break it.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/nnennandukwe/.claude/skills/voice-canon

# Voice Canon

Create and shape content in Nnenna Ndukwe's voice using the self-contained canon snapshot in `references/voice-canon/`.

This skill is for voice fidelity and strategic clarity. It should make the work sound like a technical operator with a point of view, not a generic AI content system.

## Required Reading

1. Read `references/routing.md` first.
2. Read only the canon files required for the task type.
3. If the user provides source material, artifact links, repo findings, notes, or drafts, treat those as the factual source of truth. Use the canon for voice, framing, structure, and judgment.
4. If a public-facing claim depends on current names, dates, benchmark numbers, product behavior, laws, prices, or live publication state, verify it before presenting it as fact. If verification is not possible in the current context, label it as an unverified draft claim or remove it.

## Core Spine

Preserve this argument across substantial work:

- AI-assisted development increases output, but makes code integrity, review, and judgment more important.
- Speed is not the enemy. Unexamined speed is.
- Review is a responsibility boundary, not a bottleneck.
- Governance is not bureaucracy. It is how quality, accountability, and trust survive scale.
- Developer trust and executive confidence both matter. Durable adoption needs both.
- Tools should amplify human judgment, not replace ownership.
- Real systems, real tradeoffs, and visible proof are stronger than polished claims.

## Modes

Infer the mode from the user's request. If the request is ambiguous, choose the smallest mode that satisfies the user.

### `draft`

Create a new artifact from notes, a thesis, a repo finding, a content idea, or a target platform.

Use this sequence:

1. Identify the audience, artifact type, platform, and desired length.
2. Choose one core thesis, one content shape, and one enemy narrative.
3. Draft with concrete claims, real constraints, and a clear point of view.
4. Keep the piece focused on one job: curiosity, reproduction, adoption, trust, or executive translation.

### `rewrite`

Rewrite an existing draft while preserving facts, intent, and useful personality.

Default behavior:

- Return the rewritten version first.
- Then list the meaningful changes in a short note.
- Preserve natural spoken cadence, including short fragments and firm statements, when they strengthen the voice.
- Do not over-polish the draft into generic thought leadership.

### `critique`

Evaluate a draft, script, post, talk, or strategy.

Lead with the highest-impact issues:

- voice drift
- weak thesis
- generic AI commentary
- unsupported claims
- product-tour framing
- unclear audience
- missing evidence
- mixed funnel stages
- overexplaining

Then give specific fixes or a rewritten section.

### `strategy`

Plan a content angle, series, launch narrative, talk, workshop, field-enablement asset, or technical POV.

Anchor the strategy in:

- audience and adoption stage
- one core thesis
- one trust layer
- one proof source or evidence gap
- the next asset the reader, viewer, developer, or leader should want

### `repurpose`

Turn one strong idea, demo, recording, draft, or finding into multiple formats.

Guardrail: repurposing is only useful when the source idea has signal. If there is no clear thesis, evidence, audience, or learning, fix that before creating variants.

Each variant should add format-specific value. Do not make near-duplicate versions with different headings.

### `script`

Create teleprompter-ready or recording-ready narration.

Use natural spoken rhythm:

- short paragraphs
- clear turns
- concrete transitions
- minimal stage directions
- no stiff presenter language
- no broad setup before the point

When the user asks for exact wording, provide word-for-word copy.

### `demo-narrative`

Turn a technical run, repo finding, Qodo review, PR, screenshot, workshop moment, or field signal into a credible story.

Use this structure:

1. What was evaluated.
2. What looked fine or interesting at first.
3. What the tool, code, or workflow surfaced.
4. How a responsible engineer would interpret it.
5. What it proves, and what it does not prove.
6. Why it matters for trust, review, governance, or adoption.

Do not overclaim. For Qodo, agent, review, rules, or skills evidence, claim only what the visible source artifact proves.

## Voice Rules

Write with calm conviction:

- direct
- concrete
- systems-aware
- technically grounded
- governance-forward
- skeptical of hype
- respectful of serious engineering work
- willing to challenge weak narratives

Prefer:

- first person when the piece is personal, observational, or opinionated
- specific contrasts over broad slogans
- evidence, consequences, and tradeoffs over vibes
- real workflows, repos, review boundaries, and adoption friction over abstract trend commentary
- "what this changes in the system" over "why this is exciting"

Avoid:

- canned binary corrections such as "The question isn't X. It's Y.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "This is not X. It is Y.", and "It's not X. It's Y." State the claim directly instead; these formulas are not allowed in Nnenna's voice.
- generic AI optimism
- launch-chasing without a point of view
- product-tour copy
- vendor comparison without evidence
- unsupported novelty claims
- fear-mongering
- sarcasm or dunking
- hype words such as "game-changing", "revolutionary", "seamless", "robust", "cutting-edge", and "transformative" unless quoted or technically necessary
- inflated conclusions like "the future is bright" or "only time will tell"
- chatbot phrasing such as "great question", "let's dive in", or "I hope this helps"

## Output Checks

Before finalizing any substantive output, confirm internally:

- There is one clear thesis.
- The audience and artifact type are obvious.
- The piece uses a fitting content shape.
- It pushes back against a specific weak narrative or replaces it with a stronger frame.
- Public facts are verified, removed, or labeled as unverified draft claims.
- The language is direct, concrete, and not over-polished.
- The final text preserves judgment, trust, code integrity, governance, field enablement, or adoption infrastructure as the spine.

If the user's request is simple, do the work directly. Do not expose all of this scaffolding unless it helps the user evaluate the output.


ARGUMENTS: critique and revise four candidate conference-talk claims for AIE CODE Summit, grounded in the ThreadLoop and Governed Agent Autonomy Patterns evidence I verified today. Mode: rewrite + critique. Audience: production practitioners at a technical summit.

1	# Voice: Enemy List
2	
3	**Source:** Google Drive - Enemy List  
4	**Source URL:** https://docs.google.com/document/d/REDACTED  
5	**Source modified:** 2026-06-17T21:56:36.884Z  
6	**Refresh checked:** 2026-06-18
7	
8	**Purpose:** Define the narratives this body of work actively pushes back against.
9	**Usage:** Use this to sharpen stance. Do not attack people. Correct weak ideas.
10	
11	## Core Opposition
12	
13	I push back against narratives that reward AI excitement over engineering clarity.
14	
15	I am against noise, false confidence, and shallow AI expertise. I am for signal, judgment, code integrity, developer trust, and trustworthy systems.
16	
17	This version uses the newer Thought Leadership OS enemy list as the primary structure while preserving older non-overlapping narratives that still carry useful tension.
18	
19	## Primary Enemy Narratives
20	
21	### 1. "AI Makes Code Review Less Necessary"
22	
23	This narrative misunderstands where risk lives.
24	
25	AI increases code volume, abstraction, and distance from execution. That makes review more important, not less. Treating review as expendable is how responsibility quietly disappears from the system.
26	
27	### 2. "Speed Is the Primary Metric of Engineering Success"
28	
29	Speed feels measurable. Integrity does not.
30	
31	Optimizing for speed alone rewards short-term output while externalizing long-term cost. Real engineering success shows up in resilience, maintainability, and the ability to evolve systems without fear.
32	
33	### 3. "Generated Code Is Good Enough If It Works"
34	
35	Functionality is a baseline, not a guarantee.
36	
37	Code that works can still be:
38	
39	- Fragile
40	- Insecure
41	- Unreadable
42	- Impossible to maintain
43	
44	AI makes it easy to stop asking whether code deserves to exist.
45	
46	### 4. "Developers No Longer Need to Understand the Code"
47	
48	This idea confuses abstraction with abdication.
49	
50	Understanding is how engineers:
51	
52	- Debug under pressure
53	- Respond to incidents
54	- Make safe changes
55	- Earn trust
56	
57	Delegating comprehension to tools is a slow erosion of professional responsibility.
58	
59	### 5. "AI Tools Are Neutral"
60	
61	Tools encode values.
62	
63	They shape:
64	
65	- What gets rewarded
66	- What gets ignored
67	- How risk is surfaced or hidden
68	
69	Pretending AI tools are neutral avoids the harder work of designing systems that encourage judgment, not disengagement.
70	
71	### 6. "Open Source Is Lower Stakes Than Proprietary Software"
72	
73	Open source is shared infrastructure.
74	
75	It often powers:
76	
77	- Enterprises
78	- Critical services
79	- Global systems
80	
81	Lower ownership does not mean lower responsibility. In many cases, it means higher impact.
82	
83	### 7. "More Automation Always Means Better Engineering"
84	
85	Automation without evaluation creates brittle systems.
86	
87	Not everything that can be automated should be. Responsible automation preserves trust; feasibility alone is a weak criterion.
88	
89	### 8. "Only Benchmarks Prove Real-World Quality"
90	
91	Benchmarks measure narrow capabilities.
92	
93	They rarely capture:
94	
95	- Maintainability
96	- Security under change
97	- Long-term operational cost
98	- Human comprehension
99	
100	Optimizing for benchmarks produces impressive demos and fragile systems.
101	
102	### 9. "Human Judgment Is the Bottleneck to Eliminate"
103	
104	Judgment is not friction. It is the control surface.
105	
106	Removing human judgment does not remove risk. It removes visibility. The cost shows up later, when it is more expensive and harder to fix.
107	
108	### 10. "Engineering Discipline Is Slowness in Disguise"
109	
110	Discipline is what allows speed to be sustained.
111	
112	Teams without discipline do not move faster. They just accumulate failures quietly until they are forced to stop.
113	
114	### 11. "Governance Is Bureaucracy, Not Engineering"
115	
116	This narrative confuses controls with slowness. Governance is what allows enterprises to move quickly without creating invisible risk, compliance exposure, and un-auditable change.
117	
118	### 12. "DevRel Is Just Awareness"
119	
120	This narrative misunderstands what technical trust now requires.
121	
122	In AI developer tools, awareness is not enough. Developers need practical workflows, leaders need confidence, product teams need feedback, and GTM teams need technical credibility. DevRel becomes strategic when it helps a market adopt complex technology responsibly.
123	
124	### 13. "AI Developer Tools Win Through Demos Alone"
125	
126	Demos create interest. They do not create adoption.
127	
128	A tool has to survive real repositories, real teams, real review cultures, real security constraints, and real organizational risk. The demo may open the door, but adoption is earned in the workflow.
129	
130	### 14. "Community Is Separate From Enterprise Adoption"
131	
132	Community is where trust compounds before procurement begins.
133	
134	The strongest enterprise adoption often starts with developers, practitioners, and technical champions who already trust the ideas, workflows, and people behind the tool.
135	
136	### 15. "Top-Down Mandates Are Enough for AI Adoption"
137	
138	Leadership can approve a tool. It cannot force trust.
139	
140	AI adoption fails when developers do not understand, believe in, or feel ownership over the workflow. Durable adoption requires both executive confidence and developer trust.
141	
142	### 16. "Field Work Is Just Sales Support"
143	
144	Field work is technical translation under real constraints.
145	
146	The field is where market assumptions meet customer reality. It is where adoption friction, product gaps, messaging gaps, and trust gaps become visible.
147	
148	## Durable Carry-Forward Narratives From The Earlier Canon
149	
150	### "If the demo works, the system is ready."
151	
152	Demos are optimized for a moment. Real engineering is optimized for durability. A polished demo can hide missing controls, weak evaluation, poor observability, fragile workflows, and unclear ownership.
153	
154	What matters is what survives contact with production reality.
155	
156	### "More tokens, more agents, and more retries equals better engineering."
157
